evidenceAudit.scope: Head injury and traumatic brain injury in adults and children in India from prehospital care to discharge: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) grading, airway, breathing and circulation, computed tomography (CT) indications, admission and surgical criteria, raised intracranial pressure (ICP) treatment, seizure prophylaxis and discharge, built on the ICMR Neurosurgery STW for Head Injury (July 2024).
findings: GCS bands (13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate, 3–8 severe), CT indications, red flags, prehospital ABC and transfer, admission criteria, extradural haematoma above 30 cc and subdural haematoma above 10 mm with midline shift above 5 mm for surgery, PaCO2 30–35 mmHg, head-end elevation, mannitol 20% 200 mL (adults) only if systolic BP above 90 mmHg, mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg, 3% saline 3 mL/kg 8-hourly, phenytoin 20 mg/kg then 5 mg/kg/day, levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily for 1–3 months, steroids not useful, repeat CT at 24 hours checked against the ICMR Neurosurgery STW (July 2024).

Tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours within 3 hours for GCS 12 or less or intracranial bleed on CT checked against the CFPC CRASH-3 summary; BTF 4th edition BP, ICP, CPP, hyperventilation, steroid and seizure-prophylaxis statements from a Medical Dialogues summary.
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: The STW gives no SpO2 or blood-pressure target beyond systolic above 90 mmHg before mannitol.
The ICMR STW gives no tranexamic acid or analgesic doses; tranexamic acid is from the CRASH-3 summary (CFPC) and analgesia from the morphine label and a UK paediatric guideline.
BTF 4th edition targets were read in a secondary summary.
Anticoagulant reversal agents are named for referral only; no opened source gives a reversal regimen.
Intubation at GCS 8 or less is standard practice, not stated in the cited sources.
Children's mannitol dose is described as weight-based without a number; the 0.25–1 g/kg range is used.
The STW gives two PaCO2 ranges (30–35 and 30–32 mmHg); 30–35 mmHg is shown.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of death and disability among young people in India, mostly from road traffic crashes and falls. The primary injury happens at impact; much of the harm that follows is secondary injury from hypoxia, hypotension, raised intracranial pressure and seizures, which good early care prevents. The ICMR workflow asks for ABC stabilisation in the golden hour, a search for other injuries, GCS grading, early non-contrast CT with cervical spine imaging, admission for those at risk, osmotherapy for clinical signs of raised ICP once systolic BP is above 90 mmHg, and urgent neurosurgical referral for operable haematomas. Tranexamic acid given within 3 hours reduces head-injury death in patients with mild to moderate injury (CRASH-3), so timing of arrival matters as much as the scan.
keyMechanisms: Primary injury: contusion, diffuse axonal injury and haematomas at impact.
Secondary injury: hypoxia, hypotension, hypercarbia and seizures worsen brain damage.
Expanding haematoma or oedema raises ICP and reduces cerebral perfusion, leading to herniation.
Osmotic agents draw water out of the brain to lower ICP.

symptoms: Vomiting (persistent vomiting is a CT indication) (ICMR STW)
physicalSigns: Scalp wound, skull fracture, cerebrospinal fluid leak
redFlags: Unconscious; irregular respiration; asymmetric pupils (ICMR STW)
Falling GCS, new focal deficit (ICMR STW)
Bradycardia with hypertension (Cushing response) (ICMR STW)
Persistent vomiting or restlessness (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Road traffic crashes, often without helmet

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Often coexists with head injury; never let it explain a low GCS — CT the head and recheck GCS as levels fall.
Low capillary glucose that corrects with dextrose; check glucose in every patient with reduced consciousness.

differentials.condition: Stroke or intracranial haemorrhage causing the fall
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Focal deficit out of proportion to trauma or sudden onset before the fall; CT and CT angiography settle it.
Witnessed seizure before the fall, tongue bite, gradual recovery of GCS; CT still needed if injury occurred.
Neck pain, tenderness or neurological deficit; immobilise and image the cervical spine with the head CT (ICMR STW).
History inconsistent with injuries, delayed presentation, multiple bruises of different ages; skeletal survey and safeguarding.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Mild 13–15; moderate 9–12; severe 3–8.
GCS below 15, transient loss of consciousness, suspected skull fracture, post-traumatic seizure, focal deficit, persistent vomiting, amnesia.
Extradural haematoma above 30 cc; subdural haematoma above 10 mm thick with midline shift above 5 mm and deterioration.
GCS 12 or less, or intracranial bleeding on CT, without major extracranial bleeding, within 3 hours of injury.
Systolic BP 100 mmHg or more (age 50–69) or 110 mmHg or more (15–49 or over 70); treat ICP above 22 mmHg; CPP 60–70 mmHg.

clinicalManagement.title: Prehospital and arrival
actions: ABC per trauma guidelines; control external bleeding; immobilise the cervical spine (ICMR STW).
Transfer once ABC stable to a centre with CT and a neurosurgeon (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Anticoagulants, antiplatelets and wounds
actions: Ask about warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants and antiplatelets; CT all anticoagulated patients and arrange urgent reversal with haematology if bleeding.
Clean and close scalp wounds; tetanus toxoid 0.5 mL IM if not already given (DGHS STG).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and image
actions: GCS, pupils, focal signs; search for other injuries (ICMR STW).
Non-contrast CT head with cervical spine imaging (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Raised ICP
actions: Elevate the head end; sedation and analgesia; PaCO2 30–35 mmHg if ventilated (ICMR STW).
Mannitol only if systolic BP above 90 mmHg and red flags; or 3% saline (ICMR STW).
Steroids are not useful (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Tranexamic acid and analgesia
actions: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours if GCS 12 or less or bleeding on CT, within 3 hours (CRASH-3).
Pain relief with paracetamol and titrated IV morphine; avoid oversedation that masks a falling GCS.

clinicalManagement.title: Severe TBI in the intensive care unit (ICU)
actions: Keep systolic BP 100–110 mmHg or more by age; treat ICP above 22 mmHg; CPP 60–70 mmHg (BTF).
Avoid prolonged hyperventilation to PaCO2 25 mmHg or less; no steroids (BTF).
Phenytoin for early seizures (first 7 days); start feeding by day 5–7 (BTF).

clinicalManagement.title: Surgery
actions: Extradural above 30 cc or subdural above 10 mm with shift above 5 mm and deterioration: neurosurgery (ICMR STW).
Decompressive craniectomy by a neurosurgeon only (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Admit or discharge
actions: Admit: amnesia, loss of consciousness, falling consciousness, moderate–severe headache, intoxication, skull fracture, other injury or abnormal CT (ICMR STW).
Others: discharge with head-injury advice and return precautions (ICMR STW).

vignette.text: A 27-year-old motorcyclist without a helmet is brought to a district hospital in Bihar 90 minutes after colliding with a tractor. He was unconscious for about 2 minutes, has vomited twice and smells of alcohol. GCS is 12 (E3 V4 M5), pupils are equal and reactive, BP 132/84 mmHg, pulse 96/min and SpO2 97% on air. There is a boggy scalp swelling over the left temple. The nearest CT scanner is 70 km away.

guidedApproach.title: Primary and secondary brain injury
guidedApproach.prompt: Why does early care change outcome when the impact has already happened?
guidedApproach.guidance: The damage at impact — contusion, axonal shearing and haematoma — cannot be undone, but much of the disability after head injury comes from secondary injury in the hours that follow. Hypoxia, hypotension, hypercarbia, hypoglycaemia, seizures and an expanding haematoma all reduce oxygen delivery to brain tissue that is already vulnerable. A single episode of hypotension or hypoxia during transfer is associated with worse outcome. This is why the workflow insists on stabilising airway, breathing and circulation before transfer, and why a falling GCS, a widening pupil or the Cushing response (bradycardia with hypertension) are emergencies: they signal rising intracranial pressure and impending herniation. Tranexamic acid works on the same principle — it limits haematoma growth when given within 3 hours.

guidedApproach.title: Reading the GCS and the red flags
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you recognise the patient who is getting worse?
guidedApproach.guidance: Record the GCS by its components (eye, verbal, motor), because a change in motor score is the most reliable sign of deterioration. Mild injury is GCS 13–15, moderate 9–12 and severe 3–8. A drop of even one or two points, a new focal deficit, unequal pupils, persistent vomiting, worsening headache or restlessness all mean the brain is under threat. Alcohol is common in Indian road-traffic injuries and is a trap: an intoxicated patient with a low GCS must be scanned and reassessed, never assumed to be 'just drunk'. Always look for associated injuries to the chest, abdomen, pelvis and long bones, because blood loss elsewhere causes the hypotension that harms the brain.

guidedApproach.title: Who needs a CT and when
guidedApproach.prompt: Which patients need imaging, and what does the scan decide?
guidedApproach.guidance: Non-contrast CT of the head with cervical spine imaging is the key test and should be done as soon as possible in anyone who is not completely asymptomatic. The workflow lists definite indications: GCS below 15, any loss of consciousness, suspected skull fracture, post-traumatic seizure, a focal deficit, persistent vomiting or amnesia. The CT answers three questions: is there a lesion that needs surgery (an extradural haematoma above 30 cc, or a subdural above 10 mm with midline shift above 5 mm and deterioration); does the patient need admission; and is there bleeding that makes tranexamic acid worthwhile. Where the scanner is far away, stabilise first, give tranexamic acid if within 3 hours and GCS is 12 or less, and transfer with monitoring.

guidedApproach.title: Protecting the brain until definitive care
guidedApproach.prompt: What are the priorities for a moderate or severe head injury?
guidedApproach.guidance: Secure the airway (by standard practice, intubate if GCS is 8 or less or the airway is at risk), keep oxygen saturation and blood pressure normal — in severe injury, systolic BP of at least 100–110 mmHg depending on age — and elevate the head of the bed. Give tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours within 3 hours for GCS 12 or less or a bleed on CT. Signs of rising ICP with an adequate BP are treated with mannitol or 3% saline as a bridge to surgery; prolonged hyperventilation and steroids do not help. Phenytoin or levetiracetam is used for post-traumatic seizures. Treat pain with paracetamol and carefully titrated morphine, checking GCS and pupils before each opioid dose so that sedation does not hide deterioration.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 27-year-old man arrives 90 minutes after a motorcycle crash. He was unconscious for 2 minutes and has GCS 12 with equal pupils. BP is 132/84 mmHg and SpO2 97%. The nearest CT scanner is 70 km away, and there is no other bleeding.
boardQuestions.question: Which is the most appropriate step before transfer?

options.text: Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours
options.explanation: Correct. GCS 12 within 3 hours of injury meets CRASH-3 criteria; the infusion can run during transfer.

options.text: Give dexamethasone to reduce brain swelling
options.explanation: Steroids do not improve outcome or lower ICP in head injury (ICMR STW; BTF).
Mannitol is for clinical signs of raised ICP with systolic BP above 90 mmHg; he has none.

options.text: Wait until the CT result before any treatment
options.explanation: Tranexamic acid only helps within 3 hours; waiting for a distant CT would lose the window.

options.text: Hyperventilate to a PaCO2 of 25 mmHg
options.explanation: Prolonged hyperventilation to 25 mmHg or less is not recommended (BTF).

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Recognise the indication and time window for tranexamic acid in TBI.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: GCS 12 or less or bleed on CT, within 3 hours: tranexamic acid 1 g + 1 g.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 45-year-old woman fell from a ladder. GCS was 14 on arrival and is now 10 an hour later, with a dilating right pupil. BP 168/90 mmHg, pulse 54/min. CT shows a right extradural haematoma of 45 cc with midline shift.
boardQuestions.question: What is the best next step?

options.explanation: Observation alone is unsafe: she has a surgical lesion and signs of herniation.

options.text: Urgent neurosurgical evacuation, with mannitol as a bridge
options.explanation: Correct. An extradural haematoma above 30 cc needs surgery (ICMR STW); mannitol is appropriate with systolic BP above 90 mmHg and red flags.

options.text: Start phenytoin and repeat CT in 24 hours
options.explanation: Seizure prophylaxis does not treat an expanding haematoma; delay risks death.
Bradycardia with hypertension is the Cushing response to raised ICP; the treatment is decompression.
Lumbar puncture is dangerous with a mass lesion and raised ICP (risk of herniation).

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Identify a surgical lesion and the signs of herniation.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Extradural haematoma above 30 cc, or deterioration with shift: neurosurgery now.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 35-year-old man was assaulted and is drowsy, smells strongly of alcohol, and has GCS 13. He has a 4 cm scalp laceration over the occiput but no vomiting, and his pupils are equal. His friends say he is 'just drunk', that he often drinks this much, and want to take him home tonight.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Allow discharge with friends because the GCS is above 12
options.explanation: GCS below 15 after head injury is a CT indication (ICMR STW); alcohol does not explain it safely.

options.text: Observe until sober, then decide on imaging
options.explanation: Waiting delays the diagnosis of an intracranial bleed; intoxication is an admission criterion in itself.

options.text: CT head with cervical spine imaging and admission for observation
options.explanation: Correct. GCS below 15 mandates CT, and intoxication is an admission criterion (ICMR STW).
Naloxone has no role unless opioid toxicity is suspected; it does not exclude brain injury.
Skull X-ray does not show intracranial bleeding; CT is the test.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Do not attribute a low GCS to alcohol after head injury.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Head injury + intoxication: CT and admit; never assume 'just drunk'.

patientEducation: Return at once for drowsiness, vomiting, severe headache, seizure, weakness or confusion.
Helmet and seat-belt use.
dischargeCriteria: GCS 15, no red flags, CT normal or stable (ICMR STW)
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review for persistent headache, memory or mood symptoms; antiseizure medicine review by neurosurgeon or neurologist (ICMR STW).

title: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (India)
specialty: Infectious Diseases / Occupational Health / Emergency Medicine

evidenceAudit.scope: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) after occupational (needlestick, splash) and non-occupational (sexual, including sexual assault) exposure in India: first aid, risk assessment, timing, the three-drug regimen, baseline and follow-up tests, hepatitis B and C, and transition to pre-exposure prophylaxis. The NACO National Guidelines for HIV Care and Treatment (2021) section 2.10 could not be opened, so WHO (2024), CDC (2025) and the WHO-prequalified TLD label are used.
findings: Start as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours; 28-day course; three drugs preferred (WHO 2024 summary).

Dolutegravir plus tenofovir plus lamivudine or emtricitabine as a preferred regimen; baseline HIV, hepatitis B, creatinine, ALT, AST and pregnancy tests; HIV testing at 4–6 and 12 weeks (CDC 2025, Appendix A).

TLD (dolutegravir/lamivudine/tenofovir DF 50/300/300 mg) one tablet daily for 28 days for PEP, 30 kg or more; not with creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min; dolutegravir 50 mg twice daily with rifampicin; separate from cations (WHO PQ label HA737).

Paediatric dolutegravir weight bands and PEP dosing checked against the WHO-prequalified dispersible label (HA793); lamivudine, tenofovir and zidovudine paediatric doses against NYSDOH Table A1 (December 2025); HBIG 0.06 mL/kg, vaccine 1 mL (0.5 mL under 19) at 0, 1, 6 months, and HCV RNA at 4–6 weeks against the Kasturba Hospital guideline.
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: NACO 2021 Tables 2.10.6–2.10.11 (exposure and source codes, regimens, follow-up) could not be read; NACO-specific regimens and codes are not shown.

Children under 30 kg: no single source opened gives a complete paediatric PEP regimen; the regimen here combines the WHO-prequalified dolutegravir dispersible label (PEP dosing) with NYSDOH paediatric doses of lamivudine, zidovudine and tenofovir.
Hepatitis B PEP (HBIG 0.06 mL/kg and vaccine schedule) and first aid are from the Kasturba Hospital, Manipal occupational PEP guideline, not the national NACO tables.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: PEP is a 28-day course of antiretroviral therapy (ART) started soon after a possible exposure to HIV to stop infection becoming established. Health workers in India are at risk from needlestick and sharps injuries, and PEP is also needed after sexual exposure and sexual assault. It works best within hours and is not started after 72 hours. Care includes immediate first aid, assessing the exposure and the source, baseline testing, a three-drug regimen (dolutegravir with tenofovir and lamivudine as a single TLD tablet in India), adherence support, follow-up HIV testing, and hepatitis B and C assessment. People with ongoing risk can move straight on to pre-exposure prophylaxis. The same visit also deals with hepatitis B, for which vaccination and hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) are highly effective, and hepatitis C, for which there is no prophylaxis but early detection allows cure.
keyMechanisms: HIV first infects local cells and reaches lymph nodes over 24–72 hours.
Early ART can block viral replication before infection is established.
Integrase inhibitors (dolutegravir) block viral DNA integration; tenofovir and lamivudine block reverse transcriptase.
Risk depends on fluid, route, depth of injury and source viral load.

symptoms: Recent needlestick, sharps or mucosal splash with blood or body fluid
Recent condomless sex or sexual assault
Symptoms of acute HIV during follow-up: fever, sore throat, rash, lymph nodes
physicalSigns: Mucosal splash (eye, mouth) or non-intact skin contact
Depth of injury and visible blood on the device
redFlags: Presentation after 72 hours: PEP not indicated; test and counsel (WHO 2024)
Symptoms of acute HIV (fever, rash, sore throat) during follow-up
Creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min: TLD unsuitable (label)
Sexual assault: also emergency contraception and STI care

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: No breach of skin or mucosa; no PEP is needed for HIV or hepatitis B (Kasturba guideline risk table).
Reactive baseline HIV test before PEP; manage as HIV infection and refer to the ART centre, not PEP.

differentials.condition: Hepatitis B exposure in a non-immune person
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Source HBsAg positive or unknown with worker anti-HBs below 10 mIU/mL; needs HBIG and vaccination.
Source anti-HCV positive; no prophylaxis exists, so test HCV RNA at 4–6 weeks.

differentials.condition: Acute HIV seroconversion during or after PEP
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fever, rash or sore throat 2–6 weeks after exposure; antigen-antibody test plus HIV RNA confirms it.
Nausea, headache or rash starting after the first doses with a negative HIV test; adjust supportive treatment rather than stop.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Start ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours.
28 days.
Adults and adolescents 30 kg or more; creatinine clearance 50 mL/min or more.

vignette.text: A 24-year-old staff nurse at a medical college hospital in Pune sustains a deep needlestick injury while recapping a hollow-bore needle after drawing blood from a patient on the medical ward. The patient's HIV status is unknown, and he was admitted with weight loss and oral candidiasis. The nurse completed two doses of hepatitis B vaccine as a student but never had her anti-HBs checked. She reports 40 minutes after the injury.

guidedApproach.title: Why timing decides everything
guidedApproach.prompt: Why must PEP start within hours rather than days?
guidedApproach.guidance: After a percutaneous or mucosal exposure, HIV first infects dendritic cells and T cells at the site, then reaches regional lymph nodes and the bloodstream over roughly 24–72 hours. Antiretroviral drugs can stop this local replication before the infection becomes established, but once the virus has disseminated and integrated into host DNA, a short course cannot clear it. This is why WHO advises starting ideally within 24 hours and never after 72 hours, and why the first dose should be given before source results are available. A three-drug regimen is preferred because it suppresses replication more completely, and dolutegravir is chosen as the third drug because it is potent, well tolerated and has a high barrier to resistance.

guidedApproach.title: Assessing the exposure and the source
guidedApproach.prompt: Which exposures need PEP?
guidedApproach.guidance: Risk depends on the fluid, the route and the source. Blood and visibly blood-stained fluids carry the highest risk; deep injuries with a hollow-bore needle that was in a vein or artery carry more risk than a solid suture needle. Exposure of intact skin needs no PEP. Mucosal splashes and non-intact skin need PEP if the source is HIV positive or unknown. For sexual exposure, including sexual assault, condomless receptive anal or vaginal sex carries the highest risk. The source should be tested with consent, but PEP is started at once and stopped only if the source is shown to be HIV negative without a recent risk. Every exposure is also a hepatitis B and hepatitis C exposure.

guidedApproach.title: The baseline and follow-up tests
guidedApproach.prompt: What do you test, and when?
guidedApproach.guidance: At the first visit, test the exposed person for HIV to make sure they were not already infected, because a reactive result changes management to HIV treatment. Check hepatitis B status (HBsAg and anti-HBs), hepatitis C antibody, creatinine and transaminases for drug safety, and a pregnancy test where relevant. Follow-up HIV testing is at 4–6 weeks and again at 12 weeks; hepatitis C RNA at 4–6 weeks is used when the source is hepatitis C positive, because there is no prophylaxis and early infection can be cured. Advise condoms until follow-up tests are negative.

guidedApproach.title: Choosing and completing the regimen
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you give PEP to adults and to children?
guidedApproach.guidance: For adults and adolescents of 30 kg or more, the single-tablet combination of dolutegravir, lamivudine and tenofovir (TLD) once daily for 28 days is simple and well tolerated; separate it from antacids, calcium and iron, and check that creatinine clearance is at least 50 mL/min. Children under 30 kg need weight-based dolutegravir dispersible tablets with lamivudine and a second nucleoside (tenofovir from 2 years and 10 kg, or zidovudine for younger or smaller children), ideally under ART-centre supervision. Address hepatitis B at the same visit: a non-immune person exposed to an HBsAg-positive source needs HBIG 0.06 mL/kg and the vaccine course. Adherence support, side-effect review and follow-up testing are what make PEP effective.

title: Sexually transmitted infections: urethral discharge, genital ulcer and inguinal bubo (India)
specialty: Dermatology and Venereology / Infectious Diseases / Primary Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Syndromic management of sexually transmitted infections (STI) presenting as urethral discharge, genital ulcer disease and inguinal bubo in India, using the NACO National Technical Guidelines on STI and RTI and the NACO colour-coded STI kits, with partner management, HIV and syphilis testing and follow-up. Vaginal discharge and lower abdominal pain are in a separate topic.
findings: Syndromes and organisms (Table 3.2), dual same-day treatment of urethral discharge with ceftriaxone 500 mg IM (cefixime 800 mg oral substitute) plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days (azithromycin 1 g substitute), treatment-failure regimens for Trichomonas and Mycoplasma genitalium, 7-day follow-up and partner treatment within 60 days checked against the NACO STI/RTI guidelines (section 3.2.1, Table 3.3).

Kit contents (Kit 3 white: benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU with azithromycin 1 g; Kit 4 blue: doxycycline 100 mg × 30 with azithromycin 1 g for penicillin allergy; Kit 5 red: acyclovir 400 mg × 21 for 7 days; Kit 7 black: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days with azithromycin 1 g) checked against the NACO kit specifications (2023).
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: The opened NACO guideline text ended after urethral discharge; genital ulcer and bubo regimens come from the 2023 kit specifications.

Kit 4 doxycycline frequency was not legible (duration inferred from 30 tablets twice daily = 15 days); Kit 4 is labelled only 'GUD' — its use for penicillin allergy is inferred from its contents. Kit 5 reads three times daily for 7 days and Kit 7 twice daily for 21 days.
The NACO sections on genital ulcer, bubo, scrotal swelling and pregnancy could not be reached in the opened text; 'aspirate, do not incise' and herpetic ulcer criteria are not verified.
Kit 1 contains cefixime 400 mg, while the newer guideline table gives cefixime 800 mg; the guideline dose is shown.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: STIs are common in India and many are treated at Suraksha clinics (designated STI/RTI clinics) and primary care using syndromic management: the clinician identifies the syndrome from symptoms and signs and treats all common causes on the same day, using colour-coded NACO kits. Urethral discharge is treated for both gonorrhoea and chlamydia. Genital ulcers are treated for syphilis and chancroid (or herpes when vesicles or recurrence suggest it). Inguinal bubo is treated for lymphogranuloma venereum and chancroid. Every visit includes condom promotion, HIV and syphilis testing, partner notification and a follow-up visit. Persistent discharge after correct treatment usually means reinfection from an untreated partner, Trichomonas or Mycoplasma genitalium, and is handled with the guideline's treatment-failure regimens and referral for testing.
keyMechanisms: Gonococcal and chlamydial urethritis cause discharge and dysuria; untreated infection causes epididymitis and infertility.
Syphilis causes a painless ulcer; chancroid a painful ulcer with buboes; herpes causes recurrent painful vesicles.
Genital ulcers raise HIV transmission risk several-fold.
Single-dose directly observed treatment improves cure.

physicalSigns: Discharge at the meatus (milk the urethra if needed)
Ulcer: painless indurated (syphilis), painful ragged (chancroid), grouped vesicles (herpes)
redFlags: Persistent symptoms after 7 days: treatment failure or reinfection (NACO)
Scrotal pain with sudden onset: exclude testicular torsion
Extensive or non-healing ulcers: test for HIV
STI in a child: child protection

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Frequency, urgency and pyuria without urethral discharge; urine microscopy and culture settle it.
Sudden severe scrotal pain, high-riding testis and absent cremasteric reflex; a surgical emergency — Doppler only if it does not delay surgery.
Recurrent well-defined lesion at the same genital site after the same drug (often NSAIDs or co-trimoxazole); drug history settles it.
Recurrent oral and genital ulcers with eye or skin involvement; clinical criteria and pathergy test, negative STI tests.
Chronic painless matted inguinal nodes with weight loss; fine-needle aspiration cytology and GeneXpert settle it.
Painful grouped vesicles that recur (herpes) versus a single painless indurated ulcer (syphilis); syphilis serology and HSV PCR distinguish them.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Discharge with or without dysuria; treat for gonorrhoea and chlamydia.
Ulcer on genitals; herpetic if vesicles or recurrent, otherwise non-herpetic.

vignette.text: A 26-year-old truck driver from Namakkal attends a Suraksha clinic with 3 days of burning urination and a creamy urethral discharge. He had unprotected sex with a commercial sex worker 6 days ago and is married. He has no ulcers or groin swelling. He asks for 'one injection' and does not want his wife to know.

guidedApproach.title: Why syndromic treatment works in India
guidedApproach.prompt: Why treat several organisms at once?
guidedApproach.guidance: Most STIs present as a small number of syndromes — urethral discharge, genital ulcer, inguinal bubo, scrotal swelling — and each syndrome has a short list of common causes. Laboratory diagnosis is often unavailable or delayed in Indian primary care, and patients may not return for results. Syndromic management treats all the likely organisms on the first visit with a colour-coded kit, which cures most patients and prevents onward spread. Urethral discharge is treated for both gonorrhoea and chlamydia because they often coexist and are hard to tell apart clinically. Genital ulcers are treated for syphilis and chancroid unless vesicles or recurrence point to herpes. Ulcers raise HIV transmission risk several-fold, which is why every visit includes an HIV test.

guidedApproach.title: Examining the patient properly
guidedApproach.prompt: What must the examination include?
guidedApproach.guidance: Ask about the timing of symptoms, recent partners, condom use and previous episodes. Examine the whole genital area with good light: retract the foreskin, milk the urethra if no discharge is visible, inspect for ulcers (single or multiple, painful or painless, indurated or soft), feel the inguinal nodes, and examine the scrotum. A painful scrotal swelling of sudden onset in a young man is torsion until proved otherwise. Look in the mouth and on the skin for secondary syphilis. Partners from the previous 60 days need assessment, and the patient's wishes about disclosure must be handled with counselling rather than by skipping partner treatment.

guidedApproach.title: Tests that change management
guidedApproach.prompt: Which tests matter at a Suraksha clinic?
guidedApproach.guidance: A Gram stain of a urethral smear showing intracellular Gram-negative diplococci confirms gonorrhoea on the spot. Syphilis serology (a non-treponemal test such as RPR or VDRL with a treponemal test) and an HIV test are offered to every STI client. Nucleic acid amplification tests for gonorrhoea, chlamydia, Trichomonas and Mycoplasma genitalium, with gonococcal susceptibility testing, are needed when symptoms persist after treatment, because resistance — especially in gonorrhoea — is a growing problem in India. Scrotal Doppler ultrasound helps separate epididymitis from torsion but must never delay surgery when torsion is likely.

guidedApproach.title: Treat, prevent and follow up
guidedApproach.prompt: What does complete management look like?
guidedApproach.guidance: Give the full regimen on the day of the visit, preferably as directly observed single doses: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days for urethral discharge; benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units with azithromycin 1 g for non-herpetic ulcers (doxycycline with azithromycin if allergic to penicillin); acyclovir for herpes; and 21 days of doxycycline with azithromycin for a bubo. Promote condoms, advise abstinence until treatment is complete and partners are treated, and arrange review at 7 days. If discharge persists, ask about adherence and partners before escalating to the Trichomonas and Mycoplasma regimens and referral for testing.

Kit 2 (green: secnidazole 2 g with fluconazole 150 mg), Kit 1 (grey: cefixime 400 mg with azithromycin 1 g for cervicitis) and Kit 6 (yellow: cefixime 400 mg once with metronidazole 400 mg and doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, 28 tablets each) from the NACO kit specifications (2023).

pathophysiology.summary: Vaginal discharge is one of the commonest reasons women in India attend primary care and Suraksha clinics. Most is vaginitis — bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis or candidiasis — treated with Kit 2. Cervicitis from gonorrhoea or chlamydia is less common but causes PID, infertility and ectopic pregnancy, so women with risk factors or mucopurulent cervical discharge also get Kit 1 cover. Lower abdominal pain with cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness is treated presumptively as PID (Kit 6) once ectopic pregnancy and surgical causes are excluded. Partner treatment, HIV and syphilis testing, and follow-up at 72 hours for PID are part of care. In pregnancy, the same infections raise the risk of preterm birth, so symptomatic pregnant women are treated with regimens safe in pregnancy rather than the standard kits.
keyMechanisms: Loss of vaginal lactobacilli leads to bacterial vaginosis; Trichomonas is sexually transmitted; Candida overgrows with antibiotics, diabetes or pregnancy.
Gonorrhoea and chlamydia infect the cervix and ascend to the endometrium and tubes (PID).
Tubal scarring after PID causes infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pain.
Recurrent candidiasis (3 or more episodes a year) needs induction and suppressive treatment; most women have no predisposing condition, though diabetes should be sought (CDC).

physicalSigns: Thin grey fishy discharge (BV); frothy yellow-green (Trichomonas); curdy white (Candida)
Cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness (CDC)
redFlags: Missed period or positive pregnancy test with pain: exclude ectopic pregnancy
Fever above 38.5°C, vomiting, peritonism: admit (CDC)
Tubo-ovarian abscess (CDC)
No improvement within 72 hours (CDC)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Missed period, lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding; a positive urine pregnancy test and transvaginal ultrasound settle it.
Periumbilical pain moving to the right iliac fossa with anorexia and no cervical motion tenderness; ultrasound or computed tomography (CT) settles it.
Sudden one-sided pain, often with vomiting; pelvic ultrasound with Doppler settles it.
Frequency, dysuria and pyuria without abnormal discharge or cervical tenderness; urine microscopy and culture settle it.
Clear or white, non-offensive, no itch or pain, normal pH; reassure after a normal examination.
Blood-stained or offensive discharge, postcoital bleeding, or a retained tampon or pessary; speculum examination and VIA or Pap test settle it.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Pelvic or lower abdominal pain with cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness, no other cause.
Temperature above 38.3°C, mucopurulent discharge, raised ESR or CRP, positive gonorrhoea or chlamydia.
Surgical emergency not excluded, tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, severe illness or vomiting, temperature above 38.5°C, failure of oral therapy.

actions: Exclude pregnancy and surgical causes.

Admission criteria: IV regimen (CDC).

clinicalManagement.title: Partners and IUD
actions: Treat partners from the previous 60 days (NACO; CDC).
IUD need not be removed; consider removal if no improvement in 48–72 hours (CDC).

clinicalManagement.title: Follow-up
actions: Review PID at 72 hours; switch to IV if not better (CDC).
Retest at 3 months after gonorrhoea or chlamydia (CDC).

clinicalManagement.title: Pregnancy and recurrence
actions: Pregnant with symptomatic BV or Trichomonas: metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days; avoid secnidazole and tinidazole (CDC).
Pregnant with candidiasis: topical azole for 7 days only, no fluconazole (CDC).
Recurrent candidiasis (3 or more a year): induction then weekly fluconazole for 6 months; check glucose (CDC).

vignette.text: A 28-year-old woman from a village near Nashik, married with two children and a copper IUCD inserted 2 weeks ago, presents with 4 days of lower abdominal pain, foul-smelling discharge and dyspareunia. Temperature is 38.0°C, pulse 96/min. She has cervical motion tenderness and right adnexal tenderness but no mass. The urine pregnancy test is negative. She is eating and drinking normally.

guidedApproach.title: From the vagina to the tubes
guidedApproach.prompt: Why does it matter whether the cervix is involved?
guidedApproach.guidance: Vaginal discharge has two very different sources. Vaginitis — bacterial vaginosis, Trichomonas and Candida — is an infection or imbalance of the vagina itself; it causes symptoms but rarely serious harm, except that bacterial vaginosis and Trichomonas raise the risk of preterm birth in pregnancy. Cervicitis from gonorrhoea or chlamydia is less common but more dangerous, because these organisms ascend through the cervix to the endometrium and tubes. Pelvic inflammatory disease scars the tubes and causes infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain, which is why clinicians keep a low threshold for diagnosing and treating it. The first 3 weeks after IUD insertion carry the highest PID risk.

guidedApproach.title: Examining the woman with discharge or pain
guidedApproach.prompt: Which findings change the diagnosis?
guidedApproach.guidance: The character of the discharge helps: thin grey and fishy suggests bacterial vaginosis, frothy yellow-green suggests Trichomonas, and thick white with itch suggests Candida. A speculum examination shows whether the cervix is inflamed or producing mucopurulent discharge, which points to cervicitis. Bimanual examination is essential when there is pain: cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness is enough to treat presumptively for PID once other causes are excluded. Always test for pregnancy first — ectopic pregnancy is the must-not-miss diagnosis — and look for appendicitis, ovarian torsion and urinary infection. Fever above 38.5°C, vomiting, a mass or pregnancy mean admission.

guidedApproach.title: Bedside tests and when to scan
guidedApproach.prompt: What helps at the bedside?
guidedApproach.guidance: Vaginal pH above 4.5, a positive whiff test and clue cells on a wet mount support bacterial vaginosis; motile trichomonads confirm Trichomonas; and budding yeast or hyphae confirm Candida. A urine pregnancy test is mandatory in every woman with lower abdominal pain. Where available, nucleic acid amplification tests for gonorrhoea and chlamydia, and HIV and syphilis tests, should be done for every woman with PID. Transvaginal ultrasound is used for severe disease, a palpable mass or failure to improve, to look for a tubo-ovarian abscess. A raised C-reactive protein or white cell count supports the diagnosis but a normal value does not exclude it.

guidedApproach.title: Treat the syndrome, the pregnancy and the partner
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you choose the regimen?
guidedApproach.guidance: Non-pregnant women with vaginitis receive Kit 2 (secnidazole 2 g with fluconazole 150 mg). Mucopurulent cervicitis or high STI risk adds cover for gonorrhoea and chlamydia. Mild to moderate PID is treated as an outpatient for 14 days with a single cephalosporin dose plus doxycycline and metronidazole, with review at 72 hours; women who meet admission criteria get ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily with the same oral partners until improved. An IUD does not need to be removed unless she fails to improve in 48–72 hours. Pregnant women need different drugs: metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days for bacterial vaginosis or Trichomonas, and a 7-day topical azole for Candida — never fluconazole or secnidazole. Treat sexual partners for PID and Trichomonas; routine partner treatment is not needed for bacterial vaginosis.

evidenceAudit.scope: Long-term outpatient care of adults with compensated and decompensated cirrhosis in India: diagnosis and staging (liver stiffness, clinically significant portal hypertension, MELD), treatment of the cause (alcohol, hepatitis B and C, MASLD), non-selective beta-blockers to prevent variceal bleeding and decompensation, variceal and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) surveillance, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) prevention, nutrition, vaccination and transplant referral. Built on NICE NG50, AASLD portal hypertension guidance (2023), a Baveno VII summary, BSG/BASL ascites (2020), AASLD/EASL hepatic encephalopathy (2014), the ICMR ALF/ACLF STW and NVHCP hepatitis B and C guidelines, because no Indian national cirrhosis guideline with doses could be opened.
findings: Transient elastography, hepatology referral, MELD every 6 months (12 or more = high risk), ultrasound with or without alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) every 6 months, endoscopy at diagnosis unless starting a beta-blocker and every 3 years if no varices, carvedilol first choice (start 6.25 mg/day) and propranolol second (start 40 mg twice daily), band ligation if beta-blockers not tolerated, carvedilol avoided in refractory ascites, selective SBP prophylaxis (ascitic protein 15 g/L or less, Child-Pugh above 9 or MELD above 16) checked against NICE NG50.

Carvedilol 12.5 mg/day target, dose reduction if systolic BP below 90 mmHg, switch to propranolol or nadolol if low BP limits carvedilol, endoscopy every 2 years (active disease), 3 years (controlled) or yearly (decompensated) when off beta-blockers, no screening endoscopy needed on a beta-blocker, band ligation every 2–4 weeks to obliteration then at 6 months and yearly, checked against the AASLD 2023 guidance (slide summary).

Clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) defined as HVPG 10 mmHg or more and very likely with liver stiffness 25 kPa or more; beta-blockers to prevent decompensation in CSPH; screening endoscopy avoidable with liver stiffness below 20 kPa and platelets above 150 × 10⁹/L, checked against the Berzigotti summary of Baveno VII.

Spironolactone 100–400 mg and furosemide 40–160 mg, salt restriction, albumin after large-volume paracentesis and norfloxacin 400 mg or ciprofloxacin 500 mg daily SBP prophylaxis checked against BSG/BASL 2020 (recommendations 4.1–4.2, 2.8).

Lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools a day and rifaximin added after a second episode of hepatic encephalopathy checked against AASLD/EASL 2014 (recommendations 25–28); lactulose 20–30 mL 6-hourly and rifaximin 400 mg three times daily from the ICMR ALF/ACLF STW.

Energy 35–40 kcal/kg/day (ideal body weight), protein 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day and a late-night snack from AASLD/EASL 2014 recommendations 30–32; hepatitis B vaccination indicated in chronic liver disease (adult 1.0 mL doses at 0, 1–2 and 4–6 months) from Immunize.org and CDC.
Not clinically reviewed.

pathophysiology.summary: Cirrhosis is the end stage of chronic liver injury, in which fibrosis and regenerative nodules replace normal liver architecture. In India the commonest causes are alcohol, hepatitis B and C, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD); autoimmune hepatitis and Wilson disease are less common. Its course has two phases. In compensated cirrhosis patients feel well for years, and the main determinant of outcome is portal hypertension: once the hepatic venous pressure gradient reaches 10 mmHg (clinically significant portal hypertension, CSPH) the risk of varices, ascites and death rises. Decompensation — ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy or jaundice — marks a sharp fall in survival. Long-term care therefore has four aims: remove the cause, lower portal pressure with carvedilol before decompensation, detect varices and HCC early, and prevent and treat complications while protecting nutrition and kidneys. Patients whose MELD score rises or who decompensate should be referred early for transplant assessment.
keyMechanisms: Hepatocyte injury activates stellate cells, which lay down collagen; fibrosis and nodules raise intrahepatic vascular resistance (portal hypertension).
Portal hypertension opens portosystemic collaterals (oesophageal and gastric varices) and causes splenomegaly with low platelets.
Splanchnic vasodilation lowers effective arterial volume, activating renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and causing sodium retention, ascites, hyponatraemia and hepatorenal syndrome.
Gut bacterial translocation and impaired immunity cause SBP and other infections; ammonia and inflammation cause hepatic encephalopathy.
Non-selective beta-blockers reduce portal inflow (cardiac output and splanchnic vasoconstriction); carvedilol also lowers intrahepatic resistance through alpha-1 blockade.
Ongoing injury and regeneration in a cirrhotic liver drive hepatocellular carcinoma, especially with hepatitis B.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Common in India: varices and splenomegaly with normal liver function and normal or only mildly raised liver stiffness; Doppler shows portal vein block in EHPVO.

Fever and weight loss with exudative lymphocytic ascites (SAAG below 11 g/L); ascitic ADA and laparoscopy confirm.
Low SAAG ascites with malignant cytology; CT shows peritoneal deposits.
Generalised oedema with heavy proteinuria and low albumin; urine protein-creatinine ratio settles it.

clinicalManagement.title: Treat the cause
actions: Complete alcohol abstinence with de-addiction support and relapse-prevention medicines (see Alcohol use disorder topic).
Antiviral treatment for hepatitis B or C (NVHCP); weight loss and metabolic control for MASLD.
Refer every patient with cirrhosis to a hepatologist (NICE 1.1.9).

clinicalManagement.title: Stage the disease
actions: Elastography, platelets, MELD; look for decompensation (NICE 1.2.2; Baveno summary).
CSPH likely (stiffness 25 kPa or more or varices): start a beta-blocker (Baveno summary).

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent bleeding and decompensation
actions: Carvedilol first choice; propranolol second (NICE 1.3.3).
Titrate to heart rate and BP; reduce if systolic below 90 mmHg (AASLD).
Band ligation if beta-blockers are not tolerated or contraindicated (NICE 1.3.5).

clinicalManagement.title: Surveillance
actions: Ultrasound with or without AFP for HCC; not for people receiving end-of-life care (NICE 1.2.4–1.2.5).
Endoscopy only if not on a beta-blocker: every 2–3 years, yearly if decompensated (NICE; AASLD).

clinicalManagement.title: Complications
actions: Ascites: salt restriction, spironolactone with or without furosemide; albumin 8 g per litre after paracentesis over 5 L; SBP prophylaxis in high-risk patients (BSG/BASL; NICE 1.3.7).
Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose; add rifaximin after a recurrence (AASLD/EASL).
Avoid NSAIDs, sedatives, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and aminoglycosides in ascites.
Portal vein thrombosis on ultrasound: refer to hepatology for anticoagulation assessment.

clinicalManagement.title: Nutrition and vaccination
actions: Energy 35–40 kcal/kg/day (ideal body weight), protein 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day and a late-night snack; do not restrict protein in encephalopathy (AASLD/EASL 30–32).
Vaccinate against hepatitis B if non-immune (adult 3-dose schedule); offer hepatitis A, pneumococcal and influenza vaccines as per national guidance.

clinicalManagement.title: Refer for transplant assessment
clinicalManagement.timeframe: When MELD rises or after decompensation
actions: Specialist hepatology centre for complications or high risk (NICE 1.2.1).
Refractory ascites, recurrent encephalopathy, jaundice or HCC: transplant centre.

learningObjectives: Stage cirrhosis using elastography, platelets and MELD, and recognise clinically significant portal hypertension.
Start and titrate carvedilol to prevent bleeding and decompensation, and know when to choose band ligation.

vignette.text: Mr R, a 52-year-old auto-rickshaw driver from Kanpur, drank about 90 g of alcohol daily for 20 years and stopped six months ago. He has no symptoms. Ultrasound for dyspepsia showed a nodular liver and a 14 cm spleen. Platelets are 98 × 10⁹/L, bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, INR 1.3, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL and sodium 136 mmol/L. Liver stiffness is 31 kPa. He asks whether he needs a 'camera test' and whether there is anything he can do to stay well.

guidedApproach.title: Why portal pressure drives the outcome
guidedApproach.prompt: Why does a patient with normal liver function tests still carry a high risk?
guidedApproach.guidance:
Liver function tests measure hepatocyte injury and synthetic capacity, but they do not measure portal pressure. In cirrhosis, fibrosis and regenerative nodules distort the sinusoids and raise intrahepatic resistance, and blood flow into the portal system rises at the same time because the splanchnic vessels dilate. Once the hepatic venous pressure gradient reaches 10 mmHg, collaterals open, varices form, and the kidneys start retaining sodium. This threshold is called clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH). It is the strongest predictor of the first decompensation — ascites, variceal bleeding or encephalopathy — and decompensation, not the cirrhosis label itself, is what shortens life.
This is why the modern approach targets portal pressure early. Carvedilol lowers portal inflow and, through alpha-1 blockade, intrahepatic resistance. Started when CSPH is likely, it lowers the risk of decompensation as well as bleeding. Removing the cause (alcohol, hepatitis B or C) also lowers portal pressure over time and can lead to clinical recompensation.

guidedApproach.title: Recognising the patient who has changed
guidedApproach.prompt: Which findings at a routine visit mean the patient is no longer compensated?
guidedApproach.guidance: Most patients with compensated cirrhosis look well, so the task at each visit is to look for the transition. New ascites (weight gain, shifting dullness, leg swelling), any black stool or haematemesis, subtle encephalopathy (sleep reversal, poor concentration, a change noticed by family, asterixis) and new jaundice each signal decompensation and change the plan. Ask specifically about alcohol, over-the-counter painkillers and sedatives, because these precipitate decompensation and are common in India. Muscle wasting is easy to miss in a patient with ascites; check the temples and thighs and ask about protein intake. A patient who decompensates should be treated for the complication, reviewed for transplant, and have the precipitant identified.

guidedApproach.title: Staging without invasive tests
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you decide who needs endoscopy and who needs a beta-blocker?
guidedApproach.guidance: Elastography and the platelet count do most of the staging. A liver stiffness of 25 kPa or more makes CSPH very likely (Baveno VII summary), so the patient gains from a beta-blocker whether or not varices are present; NICE does not offer screening endoscopy to people planning to take carvedilol or propranolol (1.2.6). When stiffness is below 20 kPa and platelets are above 150 × 10⁹/L, the chance of varices needing treatment is low and endoscopy can be skipped, with repeat elastography and platelets at follow-up. These rules apply to compensated cirrhosis; decompensated patients need endoscopy, and a patient whose beta-blocker is stopped needs yearly endoscopy (AASLD). Patients between these groups, or those who cannot take a beta-blocker, need endoscopy to find medium or large varices, which then need either a beta-blocker or band ligation. Separately, every patient with cirrhosis needs an ultrasound, with or without AFP, every 6 months for HCC, and a MELD score every 6 months; a MELD of 12 or more marks high risk and should prompt specialist referral.

guidedApproach.title: Putting the long-term plan together
guidedApproach.prompt: What does a complete cirrhosis plan contain?
guidedApproach.guidance: A complete plan has five parts. First, treat the cause: support abstinence, start tenofovir or entecavir for hepatitis B, and treat hepatitis C with sofosbuvir and velpatasvir, because removing the cause can stop progression. Second, lower portal pressure: carvedilol starting at 6.25 mg a day and aiming for 12.5 mg a day, reducing the dose if systolic BP falls below 90 mmHg and avoiding it in refractory ascites. Third, surveillance: 6-monthly ultrasound and MELD, and endoscopy only when indicated. Fourth, prevent complications: salt restriction and diuretics for ascites, antibiotic prophylaxis only for high-risk patients, lactulose after an episode of encephalopathy with rifaximin added for recurrence, and strict avoidance of NSAIDs and sedatives. Fifth, protect the patient: adequate energy and protein with a late-evening snack, hepatitis B vaccination if non-immune, and early transplant referral when MELD rises or the patient decompensates.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 52-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis, abstinent for 6 months, has no symptoms. Liver stiffness is 31 kPa and platelets are 98 × 10⁹/L. He has never bled and has no ascites. His BP is 128/78 mmHg and pulse 84/min.
boardQuestions.question: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.explanation: Correct. Stiffness of 25 kPa or more makes clinically significant portal hypertension very likely; carvedilol lowers the risk of decompensation and bleeding, so screening endoscopy would not change management.

options.text: Upper GI endoscopy before any treatment
options.explanation: Not needed first: when a beta-blocker is started because CSPH is likely, screening endoscopy does not change management (Baveno summary; NICE 1.2.6).
Band ligation is for medium or large varices when beta-blockers are not tolerated or contraindicated; it does not prevent ascites or other decompensation.
Watchful waiting is suitable only when stiffness is below 20 kPa with platelets above 150; this patient has CSPH.
Antibiotic prophylaxis is for patients with ascites at high risk of SBP; he has no ascites.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Start carvedilol when liver stiffness or other findings show clinically significant portal hypertension, without waiting for endoscopy.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Liver stiffness 25 kPa or more: carvedilol, no screening endoscopy needed.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 60-year-old woman with hepatitis B cirrhosis on tenofovir has had carvedilol 12.5 mg daily for a year. She now has tense ascites needing large-volume paracentesis every 2 weeks despite maximum diuretics. Her BP is 86/54 mmHg and creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.5 mg/dL.
boardQuestions.question: What should be done with the carvedilol?

options.explanation: Continuing exposes her to further hypotension and kidney injury: NICE advises avoiding carvedilol in refractory ascites (1.3.1), and BSG/BASL advises reducing or stopping a beta-blocker when hypotension or kidney dysfunction develops (10.2).
Higher doses lower BP further and worsen renal perfusion; the target is 12.5 mg/day.

options.text: Reduce or stop it, and refer for transplant assessment
options.explanation: Correct. Systolic BP below 90 mmHg with rising creatinine is the reason to reduce or stop the beta-blocker (AASLD; BSG/BASL 10.2); NICE also advises avoiding carvedilol in refractory ascites (1.3.1). Refractory ascites is a reason for transplant referral.

options.text: Switch to propranolol 80 mg twice daily
options.explanation: Switching to another non-selective beta-blocker at a higher dose does not solve hypotension and renal hypoperfusion.
The cited sources do not support adding a vasoconstrictor to keep a beta-blocker going; they advise reducing or stopping it.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Recognise when a beta-blocker becomes harmful in advanced cirrhosis.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Systolic BP below 90 mmHg, refractory ascites or rising creatinine: reduce or stop the beta-blocker.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 48-year-old man with compensated hepatitis C cirrhosis was cured with sofosbuvir and velpatasvir (sustained virological response) 2 years ago. He does not drink alcohol, his MELD is 8, platelets are 140 × 10⁹/L and his last ultrasound was normal. He feels well and asks if he can stop his 6-monthly liver scans now that the virus has gone.
boardQuestions.question: What is the best advice?

options.text: Stop surveillance because he is cured
options.explanation: Cure lowers but does not remove HCC risk once cirrhosis is established.

options.text: Continue ultrasound with or without AFP every 6 months
options.explanation: Correct. NICE NG50 offers 6-monthly ultrasound with or without AFP to people with cirrhosis; the cirrhosis, not active virus, sets the risk.

options.text: Switch to a yearly CT scan
options.explanation: CT is not the recommended surveillance test and adds radiation and contrast exposure.
AFP alone misses many tumours; ultrasound is the core test.

options.text: Surveillance only if he develops symptoms
options.explanation: Symptomatic HCC is usually too advanced for curative treatment.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: HCC surveillance continues after viral cure in established cirrhosis.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Every patient with cirrhosis: ultrasound with or without AFP every 6 months.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 57-year-old woman with cirrhosis and ascites was admitted last month with overt hepatic encephalopathy triggered by constipation. She recovered on lactulose. Today she is oriented, passing two soft stools a day, and her family ask whether she should avoid eating dal and eggs to protect her brain.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate advice about diet?

options.text: Restrict protein to less than 0.5 g/kg/day
options.explanation: Protein restriction worsens sarcopenia and does not prevent encephalopathy.
Unnecessary restriction worsens nutrition; protein needs are higher in cirrhosis.

options.text: Normal-to-high protein (1.2–1.5 g/kg/day), frequent meals and a late-evening snack, with lactulose continued
options.explanation: Correct. Cirrhosis is a catabolic state; adequate energy and protein with a late-evening snack prevent muscle loss, and lactulose continues as secondary prevention.

options.text: Fast overnight to rest the liver
options.explanation: Overnight fasting increases muscle breakdown in cirrhosis; a late-evening snack is advised.

options.text: Stop lactulose and start rifaximin alone
options.explanation: Rifaximin is added to lactulose after a recurrence, not substituted after one episode.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Nutrition in cirrhosis: do not restrict protein; prevent sarcopenia.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Protein 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day with a late-evening snack; keep lactulose after an episode of encephalopathy.

evidenceAudit.scope: Starting and adjusting insulin in adults with type 2 diabetes and people with type 1 diabetes in India: indications, basal insulin start and titration, adding prandial insulin, premixed insulin, targets, self-monitoring, hypoglycaemia treatment and sick-day rules, built on the ICMR Type 2 and Type 1 Diabetes STWs (July 2022) and the ADA Standards of Care 2025 section 9 for doses not in the ICMR workflows.
findings: Insulin for HbA1c above 10% added to oral agents, targets (HbA1c 7% or below; pre-meal 80–130 mg/dL; post-meal below 180 mg/dL), and monitoring checked against the ICMR Type 2 Diabetes STW (July 2022).

Total daily dose 0.25–1.0 U/kg, 40–50% basal and 50% bolus in 3 doses, hypoglycaemia with 3 teaspoons glucose, glucagon 1 mg SC/IM, 25% dextrose 1–2 mL/kg, sick-day extra regular insulin 10–15% of total daily dose every 6 hours and admission criteria checked against the ICMR Type 1 Diabetes STW (July 2022).

Basal start 0.1–0.2 U/kg/day, insulin when HbA1c above 10% or glucose 300 mg/dL or more, prandial start 4 units or 10% of basal at the largest meal, premixed twice daily option, overbasalisation signs and glucagon for everyone on insulin checked against the ADA Standards of Care 2025 section 9.

Self-titration of basal insulin by 2 units every 3 days, overbasalisation above 0.5 U/kg, prandial start of 4 units or 10% of basal with basal reduction by 4 units or 10% when HbA1c is below 8%, and prandial reduction of 10–20% for hypoglycaemia checked against the ADA Overcoming Therapeutic Inertia titration guide (2024 Standards).
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: The ICMR Type 2 STW gives no insulin doses or titration; these come from ADA 2025.
The 2-units-every-3-days titration rule and the overbasalisation threshold (above 0.5 U/kg) are from the ADA Overcoming Therapeutic Inertia guide based on the 2024 Standards.
Insulin storage and injection-technique advice is general practice.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Many Indians with type 2 diabetes need insulin, often late because of fear and cost. The ICMR workflow adds basal insulin when HbA1c is above 10% despite oral drugs; ADA 2025 also advises insulin at any stage for symptomatic hyperglycaemia, catabolic features or glucose 300 mg/dL or more. Basal insulin (NPH or glargine) is started at bedtime at 0.1–0.2 U/kg and titrated to fasting glucose; prandial insulin or twice-daily premixed insulin is added when fasting glucose is controlled but HbA1c remains high. Type 1 diabetes needs basal-bolus insulin from diagnosis. Every person on insulin needs self-monitoring, hypoglycaemia education, glucagon where available and sick-day rules. A practical rule makes self-titration safe: adjust basal insulin by 2 units every 3 days towards the fasting target, and stop escalating once the dose passes about 0.5 units/kg without control.
keyMechanisms: Type 2 diabetes progresses with declining beta-cell function, so many eventually need insulin.
Basal insulin suppresses hepatic glucose output overnight and between meals.
Prandial insulin covers meal-related glucose rises.
Too much basal insulin (overbasalisation) causes hypoglycaemia and wide glucose swings.

symptoms: Polyuria, thirst, weight loss despite treatment
Blurred vision, recurrent infections (genital candidiasis, skin)
Nocturnal sweating or morning headache (nocturnal hypoglycaemia)
physicalSigns: Low BMI or rapid weight loss despite treatment (insulin deficiency)
redFlags: Glucose 300 mg/dL or more or HbA1c above 10% with symptoms: start insulin (ADA 2025)
Ketones with glucose above 250 mg/dL: sick-day rules or admit (ICMR T1DM)
Recurrent or severe hypoglycaemia
Vomiting, poor urine output, rising ketones: admit (ICMR T1DM)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Lean adult whose oral drugs fail within months; GAD antibodies positive and C-peptide low — needs insulin early.
Common in parts of India: young, lean, recurrent abdominal pain and steatorrhoea; pancreatic calcification on X-ray or ultrasound; needs insulin and enzymes.
Afternoon and evening glucose rise on prednisolone or dexamethasone with near-normal fasting values; morning NPH or prandial insulin fits the pattern.
Weight loss, ketones and low C-peptide; needs basal-bolus insulin from diagnosis, never oral drugs alone.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Basal dose above 0.5 U/kg, bedtime-to-morning glucose fall of 50 mg/dL or more, or hypoglycaemia; add prandial insulin instead of more basal.

clinicalManagement.title: Start basal insulin
actions: Continue metformin and other oral agents unless contraindicated (ADA 2025).
Basal insulin 0.1–0.2 U/kg/day at bedtime (ADA 2025).
Teach injection, SMBG and hypoglycaemia treatment; prescribe glucagon where available (ADA 2025).

clinicalManagement.title: Titrate
actions: Patient adjusts basal dose by 2 units every 3 days until fasting glucose reaches target (80–130 mg/dL) (ADA guide; ICMR T2DM).
Any hypoglycaemia: find the cause and lower the dose (ADA guide).
Basal above 0.5 U/kg without control, or bedtime-to-morning fall 50 mg/dL or more: stop escalating basal (ADA 2025; ADA guide).

clinicalManagement.title: Intensify
clinicalManagement.timeframe: When fasting controlled but HbA1c high
actions: Add prandial insulin 4 units or 10% of basal before the largest meal (ADA 2025).
Or switch to premixed insulin twice daily (ADA 2025).

clinicalManagement.title: Adjust prandial insulin
actions: Titrate prandial dose by post-meal readings (no step size stated in the opened sources); if HbA1c below 8% when adding prandial, reduce basal by 4 units or 10% (ADA guide).
Hypoglycaemia on prandial insulin: reduce that dose by 10–20% (ADA guide).

clinicalManagement.title: Type 1 diabetes
actions: Total daily dose 0.25–1.0 U/kg: 40–50% basal, 50% bolus split before 3 meals (ICMR T1DM).
Sick days: extra regular insulin 10–15% of total daily dose every 6 hours; admit if not settling (ICMR T1DM).

clinicalManagement.title: Hypoglycaemia
actions: Below 70 mg/dL: 3 teaspoons glucose or sugar (ICMR T1DM).
Severe: glucagon 1 mg SC/IM, then 25% dextrose 1–2 mL/kg IV in hospital (ICMR T1DM).

vignette.text: Mrs S, a 54-year-old school teacher from Chennai with type 2 diabetes for 11 years, takes metformin 1 g twice daily and glimepiride 4 mg daily. She has lost 4 kg in 3 months, has nocturia, and her HbA1c is 10.8% with fasting glucose 238 mg/dL. Weight is 68 kg, eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m². She is afraid that insulin means 'the last stage' and that injections will hurt.

guidedApproach.title: Why most people with type 2 diabetes eventually need insulin
guidedApproach.prompt: Is needing insulin a failure?
guidedApproach.guidance: Type 2 diabetes is a progressive loss of beta-cell function on a background of insulin resistance. Oral drugs and lifestyle changes work while enough beta-cell function remains, but over a decade many people — and in India, often earlier and at a lower body weight — no longer make enough insulin. Weight loss, rising glucose despite good adherence and catabolic features are signs of insulin deficiency, not of poor effort. Basal insulin replaces the background insulin that suppresses glucose production from the liver overnight and between meals, which is why it lowers fasting glucose so effectively. Prandial insulin covers the glucose rise after meals. Explaining this removes the stigma that insulin is a punishment or the 'last stage'.

guidedApproach.title: Recognising when insulin is needed — and when it is too much
guidedApproach.prompt: Which features tell you to start, and which tell you to stop escalating?
guidedApproach.guidance: Start insulin when HbA1c is above 10%, glucose is 300 mg/dL or more, or the patient has symptoms such as weight loss, polyuria and thirst (ADA 2025; ICMR uses HbA1c above 10%). Look for type 1 diabetes or LADA in lean adults whose oral drugs fail early, and for fibrocalculous pancreatic diabetes in young lean patients with abdominal pain. Once on insulin, watch for overbasalisation: a basal dose above about 0.5 units/kg, a fall of 50 mg/dL or more from bedtime to morning, hypoglycaemia, or widely swinging readings. These mean the patient needs prandial cover, not more basal insulin. Night sweats, nightmares and morning headaches suggest nocturnal hypoglycaemia; a check between midnight and 2 am confirms it.

guidedApproach.title: Monitoring that makes titration safe
guidedApproach.prompt: What does the patient need to measure?
guidedApproach.guidance: Self-monitoring of blood glucose is what makes insulin safe. During basal titration the key reading is the fasting glucose each morning; when prandial insulin is added, readings 2 hours after meals guide those doses. People with type 1 diabetes test before each meal and at bedtime, with an occasional check between midnight and 2 am. HbA1c every 3 months shows whether the overall plan is working. Check ketones when glucose is above 250 mg/dL during illness. Annual creatinine and eGFR matter because insulin needs fall as kidney function declines, and the injection sites should be examined at every visit for lipohypertrophy, which causes erratic absorption.

guidedApproach.title: A stepwise insulin plan
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you start, titrate and intensify?
guidedApproach.guidance: Keep metformin and other non-insulin drugs unless contraindicated, and reduce or stop the sulfonylurea when prandial insulin is added. Start basal insulin at 0.1–0.2 units/kg at bedtime — NPH is cheaper, glargine causes less nocturnal hypoglycaemia. Teach the patient to raise the dose by 2 units every 3 days until fasting glucose reaches 80–130 mg/dL, and to lower it after any hypoglycaemia. When fasting glucose is at target but HbA1c is still high, or the basal dose exceeds about 0.5 units/kg, add 4 units (or 10% of the basal dose) of prandial insulin before the largest meal, or switch to premixed insulin twice daily. Every patient on insulin needs a hypoglycaemia plan: 3 teaspoons of glucose for mild episodes, glucagon 1 mg for severe ones, and sick-day rules.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 54-year-old school teacher with type 2 diabetes for 11 years takes metformin 1 g twice daily and glimepiride 4 mg daily with good adherence. HbA1c is 10.8%, fasting glucose 238 mg/dL, and she has lost 4 kg in 3 months with nocturia. Weight is 68 kg and eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m².
boardQuestions.question: What is the best next step?

options.text: Add a third oral drug and review in 6 months
options.explanation: Weight loss with HbA1c above 10% indicates insulin deficiency; insulin is recommended (ADA 2025; ICMR).

options.text: Start basal insulin about 7–14 units at bedtime and continue metformin
options.explanation: Correct. 0.1–0.2 U/kg for 68 kg is about 7–14 units; keep metformin (ADA 2025).

options.text: Stop all oral drugs and start basal-bolus insulin 1 U/kg/day
options.explanation: Too much, too fast: basal insulin is started first and metformin continued.

options.text: Start premixed insulin 30 units twice daily
options.explanation: An unnecessarily high starting dose with high hypoglycaemia risk.
Higher sulfonylurea doses add little and raise hypoglycaemia risk when beta-cell function is failing.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 60-year-old man on glargine has titrated to 52 units daily (weight 80 kg). Fasting glucose is 110–125 mg/dL, but HbA1c is 8.9% and he has had two episodes of hypoglycaemia at 3 am. Bedtime glucose is around 220 mg/dL.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate change?

options.explanation: He is overbasalised; more basal insulin increases nocturnal hypoglycaemia.

options.text: Switch glargine to NPH at the same dose
options.explanation: NPH increases nocturnal hypoglycaemia risk and does not address post-meal glucose.
A sulfonylurea adds hypoglycaemia risk and does not target the problem.

options.text: Reduce glargine and add prandial insulin before the largest meal
options.explanation: Correct. Basal above 0.5 U/kg (52 units for 80 kg = 0.65 U/kg), a large bedtime-to-morning fall and nocturnal hypoglycaemia signal overbasalisation; add prandial cover (ADA guide).

options.text: No change because fasting glucose is at target
options.explanation: HbA1c above goal with nocturnal hypoglycaemia needs a change.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Recognise overbasalisation and intensify with prandial insulin.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Basal above 0.5 U/kg with hypoglycaemia or large overnight fall: add prandial insulin, not more basal.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 19-year-old college student with type 1 diabetes on basal-bolus insulin (total 48 units a day) phones the clinic. He has fever and has vomited twice since morning. His glucose is 310 mg/dL and urine ketones are moderate. He can still drink fluids and asks whether he should skip insulin because he cannot eat.
boardQuestions.question: What is the correct advice?

options.text: Stop all insulin until he can eat
options.explanation: Stopping insulin precipitates diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA); insulin is never stopped on sick days (ICMR T1DM).

options.text: Continue usual insulin and add regular insulin 10–15% of the total daily dose every 6 hours, with fluids and glucose checks; come in if vomiting persists or ketones rise
options.explanation: Correct. These are the ICMR T1DM sick-day rules with admission criteria.

options.text: Take only basal insulin and no extra
options.explanation: Basal alone is not enough; he needs extra insulin to clear the ketones.
Illness raises insulin needs; halving doses risks DKA.
His glucose is already high; he needs insulin, fluids and close monitoring, not extra glucose.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Apply sick-day rules in type 1 diabetes.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Never stop insulin when ill; give extra 10–15% of TDD every 6 hours and admit if not settling.

patientEducation: Injection technique and site rotation.
Recognise and treat hypoglycaemia; carry sugar.
Never stop insulin when ill; check ketones.
lifestyleAndDiet: Regular meals matched to insulin; carbohydrate awareness; exercise planning.
dischargeCriteria: Able to inject and test glucose

title: Preterm labour and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Threatened and established preterm labour and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM) in India: diagnosis, antibiotics for P-PROM, tocolysis, antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection, place of birth and newborn readiness, using WHO antenatal corticosteroid recommendations (2022) and NICE NG25 because the MoHFW antenatal corticosteroid guideline could not be opened.
findings: Speculum diagnosis of P-PROM, oral erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for up to 10 days, no co-amoxiclav, cervical length 15 mm and fetal fibronectin 50 ng/mL thresholds from 30 weeks, nifedipine tocolysis 26–33+6 weeks, oxytocin receptor antagonist if nifedipine contraindicated, no betamimetics, corticosteroids 24–33+6 weeks with one repeat course, magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 15 minutes then 1 g/hour up to 24 hours at 24–29+6 weeks (consider to 33+6) with 4-hourly monitoring checked against NICE NG25.

Dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses or betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses at 24–34 weeks when birth is likely within 7 days, with gestation reasonably assessed and facilities for newborn care, checked against WHO 2022 recommendations 1.0–1.10.

Nifedipine 20 mg orally then 10–20 mg three to four times daily adjusted to uterine activity (GPnotebook, NICE); intrapartum GBS prophylaxis with benzylpenicillin 3 g IV then 1.8 g IV every 4 hours, cefuroxime 1.5 g for non-severe allergy and vancomycin 20 mg/kg for severe allergy (Louth Hospitals, HSE 2023).
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: The MoHFW Operational Guidelines on antenatal corticosteroids (2014) were not opened.
NICE NG25 names an oral penicillin as the alternative to erythromycin without a regimen; no row is shown, and the choice is left to the obstetrician.
Nifedipine dosing is from a GPnotebook summary of NICE guidance, and GBS prophylaxis from an Irish hospital guideline citing the HSE 2023 national guideline.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: India has the largest number of preterm births in the world, and prematurity is the leading cause of newborn death. Care aims to confirm preterm labour or membrane rupture, buy time for corticosteroids and in-utero transfer to a facility with newborn care, protect the baby's brain with magnesium sulfate before early preterm birth, and prevent infection after membranes rupture. Tocolysis is short-term only. WHO links corticosteroid use to conditions that make it safe: reliable gestational age, birth expected within 7 days, no maternal infection, and adequate care for the preterm baby. Group B streptococcus (GBS) colonisation adds to the risk of early-onset neonatal sepsis, so women in preterm labour receive intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. Every hour gained before birth helps, because it allows steroids and transfer.
keyMechanisms: Infection, inflammation, overdistension and bleeding trigger preterm labour.
Corticosteroids speed fetal lung maturation and reduce respiratory distress, brain bleed and death.
Magnesium sulfate reduces cerebral palsy risk in very preterm babies.
After membranes rupture, ascending infection (chorioamnionitis) threatens mother and baby.

physicalSigns: Pooling of amniotic fluid on speculum (NICE)
Maternal tachycardia above 100/min or fetal tachycardia (chorioamnionitis)
redFlags: Chorioamnionitis: fever, tachycardia, uterine tenderness (corticosteroids contraindicated in clinical infection, WHO)
Antepartum haemorrhage
Fetal distress
Cord prolapse after rupture

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Irregular, painless tightenings with no cervical change; from 30 weeks, cervical length above 15 mm or fibronectin 50 ng/mL or less makes preterm labour unlikely (NICE).

Constant pain, a tender hard uterus and bleeding, sometimes concealed; clinical findings and fetal monitoring settle it (see Antepartum haemorrhage topic).
Dysuria, loin pain and fever; urine microscopy and culture settle it, and infection may itself trigger preterm labour.
Fever, maternal and fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness and offensive liquor after membrane rupture; clinical diagnosis with raised white cells and CRP.
