clinicalManagement.title: Confirm and assess
actions: Gestation, contractions, cervix, membranes, infection, fetal wellbeing (NICE).
Transfer in utero to a facility with newborn care when possible.
Dysuria or bacteriuria: send urine culture and treat urinary infection with a pregnancy-safe antibiotic guided by culture (see the urinary tract infection topic).

clinicalManagement.title: P-PROM
actions: Erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for up to 10 days or until labour (NICE 1.4.1).
Do not give co-amoxiclav (NICE 1.4.3).

Suspected intrauterine infection (fever with raised white cells, fetal tachycardia or offensive liquor): IV ampicillin plus gentamicin, no tocolysis, expedite birth and inform the neonatal team (NICE 1.5; MSD Manual).

clinicalManagement.title: Corticosteroids and tocolysis
actions: Corticosteroids at 24–34 weeks when criteria are met (WHO 2022; NICE 1.9).
Nifedipine 20 mg then 10–20 mg three to four times daily at 26–33+6 weeks with intact membranes; oxytocin receptor antagonist if nifedipine contraindicated; no betamimetics (NICE 1.8; GPnotebook).
At 22+0 to 23+6 weeks, discuss corticosteroids with the woman, family and multidisciplinary team (NICE 1.9.1).
Consider one repeat course before 34+0 weeks if the first was over 7 days ago and birth is very likely within 48 hours; never more than 2 courses (NICE 1.9.4–1.9.5).

clinicalManagement.title: Neuroprotection
actions: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 15 minutes, then 1 g/hour until birth or 24 hours (NICE 1.10.4).
Check pulse, BP, respiratory rate and reflexes at least 4-hourly (NICE 1.10.5).

clinicalManagement.title: Birth
actions: Newborn resuscitation team present; delayed cord clamping where appropriate; thermal care and early breastfeeding (see newborn topics).
Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis with benzylpenicillin when indicated by risk factors (Louth Hospitals; HSE 2023).

vignette.text: Sunita, a 23-year-old primigravida at 30 weeks and 2 days by first-trimester scan, attends a district hospital in Odisha with 4 hours of regular painful tightenings every 7 minutes and lower backache. She has had burning urination for 3 days. Temperature is 37.4°C, BP 112/70 mmHg and pulse 92/min. Speculum shows no pooling of liquor and the cervix appears to be opening. The hospital has no neonatal intensive care unit; the nearest is 90 km away.

guidedApproach.title: Why preterm birth happens and why time matters
guidedApproach.prompt: What can we change once preterm labour starts?
guidedApproach.guidance: Preterm labour is the final common pathway of several processes: infection and inflammation (including urinary and ascending genital infection), overdistension from multiple pregnancy, placental bleeding, cervical insufficiency and maternal stress. Once labour is established it is difficult to stop, and tocolytics only delay birth for a few days. That delay is valuable because it allows two things that change the baby's outcome: a course of corticosteroids, which matures the fetal lungs and reduces respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage and death, and transfer of the mother to a hospital with newborn care. Magnesium sulfate given shortly before a very preterm birth protects the fetal brain and reduces cerebral palsy. After the membranes rupture, ascending infection becomes the main threat to both mother and baby.

guidedApproach.title: Recognising true preterm labour and its complications
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you tell real preterm labour from false alarms?
guidedApproach.guidance: Regular painful contractions with progressive cervical change define preterm labour. Before 30 weeks, NICE advises treating suspected preterm labour as real because the cost of missing it is high. From 30 weeks, a transvaginal cervical length of 15 mm or less, or a fetal fibronectin above 50 ng/mL, confirms it, and values above these thresholds make it unlikely. A speculum examination looking for pooled liquor diagnoses P-PROM; digital examination should be avoided after membrane rupture. Look actively for causes and complications: urinary infection, bleeding from abruption, and chorioamnionitis — maternal fever, maternal and fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness and offensive liquor — which is a contraindication to tocolysis and to delaying birth.

guidedApproach.title: Tests that guide decisions
guidedApproach.prompt: Which investigations change management?
guidedApproach.guidance: Gestational age must be reliably known before giving corticosteroids, so check the dating scan. Cervical length and fetal fibronectin help from 30 weeks but should not be combined. Urine microscopy and culture look for a treatable trigger. After P-PROM, monitor maternal temperature, pulse, white cell count and CRP for chorioamnionitis, and use fetal heart rate monitoring throughout. An obstetric ultrasound confirms presentation, liquor volume and estimated weight, which help plan the place and mode of birth, and confirms whether in-utero transfer is still safe.

guidedApproach.title: Buying time and protecting the baby
guidedApproach.prompt: What should be given, and in what order?
guidedApproach.guidance: For P-PROM, start erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for up to 10 days and avoid co-amoxiclav because of an association with necrotising enterocolitis. Give corticosteroids — dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for four doses or betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for two doses — at 24–34 weeks when birth is likely within 7 days and there is no clinical infection. With intact membranes at 26–33+6 weeks, nifedipine 20 mg followed by 10–20 mg three to four times daily delays birth long enough to complete steroids and transfer; betamimetics should not be used. When birth is expected within 24 hours at 24–29+6 weeks (consider up to 33+6), give magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 15 minutes then 1 g/hour, monitoring reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output. In established preterm labour, give benzylpenicillin for group B streptococcus and call the neonatal team.

pathophysiology.summary: Febrile seizures are the commonest seizures in childhood, affecting children aged 6 months to 5 years with fever but no brain infection or metabolic cause. Most are simple — generalised, under 15 minutes and not repeated within 24 hours — and carry an excellent prognosis with only about 1% later epilepsy risk. The key clinical task is to exclude meningitis, especially in infants and under-immunised children. Seizures over 5 minutes are treated with a benzodiazepine. Antipyretics do not prevent recurrence. Intermittent clobazam during fevers is reserved for frequent or complex seizures, and continuous drugs are rarely needed. Calm, clear counselling of parents is central. Recurrence occurs in about 30%, and is most likely when the first seizure happens before 1 year of age, with a short fever-to-seizure interval, at a low temperature, or with a family history.
keyMechanisms: The immature brain has a lower seizure threshold with rapid temperature rise.
Genetic predisposition: family history is a major risk factor.
Viral infections (including roseola and influenza) are common triggers.
Febrile seizures mark predisposition rather than cause epilepsy.

clinicalManagement.title: During the seizure
actions: Protect the airway; turn the child on the side with head extended; prevent injury (IAP).

clinicalManagement.title: Seizure over 5 minutes
actions: IV midazolam 0.2 mg/kg (maximum 5 mg), diazepam 0.3–0.5 mg/kg (maximum 10 mg) or lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg); without IV access, rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg or buccal or intranasal midazolam 0.1–0.2 mg/kg (IAP; IAP STG 2022).

clinicalManagement.title: Admit or discharge
actions: Admit complex seizures and any child with signs of CNS infection or needing a lumbar puncture (IAP).
First simple seizure over 18 months, stable, parents educated: home; IAP lists lack of reliable family support as a possible reason to admit (IAP).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat the fever source
actions: Find and treat the cause of fever (otitis, pneumonia, urinary infection, viral illness).
Paracetamol for comfort at 15 mg/kg; it does not prevent recurrence (IAP; Gloucestershire guideline).

clinicalManagement.title: Prevention
actions: Antipyretics do not prevent recurrence; use for comfort (IAP).
Intermittent clobazam (or oral or rectal diazepam) for frequent seizures, a previous complex seizure, poor access to care or seizures with risk factors (IAP).
Continuous prophylaxis rarely (IAP).

actions: Explain the benign nature, the about 30% recurrence risk and the low epilepsy risk (IAP).
Teach first aid and when to give rescue medicine or seek care; explain that fever medicine is for comfort only (IAP).

vignette.text: Ananya, a 20-month-old girl from Lucknow, is brought to the emergency department after a 3-minute generalised jerking episode at home with a temperature of 39.4°C. She had a runny nose and cough for a day. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, and 40 minutes later she is playing. She has completed all scheduled vaccines. Her father had febrile seizures as a child. Her mother asks whether this is epilepsy and whether to give fever medicine every few hours to stop another one.

guidedApproach.title: Why young children have febrile seizures
guidedApproach.prompt: What makes a 6–60 month old prone to seizures with fever?
guidedApproach.guidance: The developing brain has a lower seizure threshold, and a rapid rise in temperature during a viral illness can trigger a generalised seizure in a child who is genetically predisposed — a family history in a first-degree relative is one of the strongest risk factors. Febrile seizures are a marker of this age-limited susceptibility; they do not damage the brain and do not cause epilepsy. That is why antiseizure drugs, although they reduce recurrence, do not change the long-term outlook. The real clinical danger lies not in the seizure but in what may be causing the fever: bacterial meningitis can present with a seizure, especially in infants whose signs are subtle and in children who are not fully immunised.

guidedApproach.title: Simple versus complex, and the meningitis question
guidedApproach.prompt: Which features change your management?
guidedApproach.guidance: A simple febrile seizure is generalised, lasts under 15 minutes and does not recur within 24 hours; about 70–75% are simple. A complex seizure is focal, lasts 15–30 minutes or recurs within 24 hours; beyond 30 minutes it is febrile status epilepticus. The examination after the seizure focuses on the fever source and on signs of central nervous system infection: neck stiffness, a bulging fontanelle, a petechial rash, persistent drowsiness or a post-ictal deficit. Recurrence risk rises with age under 1 year at the first seizure, fever of less than 24 hours, a lower temperature at onset and a first-degree family history; with none of these the risk is under 15%, and with three or more it exceeds 60%.

guidedApproach.title: Less is more
guidedApproach.prompt: Which tests are needed after a febrile seizure?
guidedApproach.guidance: For most children, the only investigation needed is to find the source of fever. Lumbar puncture is standard under 6 months, should be considered at 6–12 months when Hib or pneumococcal vaccination is incomplete or unknown, and is indicated at any age with meningeal signs or when antibiotics have already been given and could mask meningitis. Blood tests (count, culture, glucose, electrolytes, calcium) and urinalysis are for when the fever source is unclear or the diagnosis uncertain. EEG has little value after a simple or first complex seizure, and neuroimaging is not routine; MRI is reserved for recurrent complex seizures with a prolonged post-ictal deficit, and CT only for suspected bleeding or a structural lesion.

guidedApproach.title: Rescue, reassurance and selective prophylaxis
guidedApproach.prompt: When do children need drugs?
guidedApproach.guidance: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes is treated with a benzodiazepine: midazolam 0.2 mg/kg, IV diazepam 0.3–0.5 mg/kg or lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, or rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg when there is no IV access. Most children need no regular medicine. Antipyretics such as paracetamol make the child comfortable but do not prevent recurrence, so parents should not wake a child to give them. Intermittent oral clobazam 0.3 mg/kg every 12 hours for 24 hours from the start of a fever is reserved for frequent or complex seizures or families far from care. Continuous valproate or phenobarbitone is rarely needed. The most important intervention is calm, clear counselling: what to do during a seizure, when to call for help, and that the outlook is excellent.

evidenceAudit.scope: Contraceptive counselling and provision under the Indian national family planning programme: injectable medroxyprogesterone acetate (Antara), combined oral contraceptive pills (Mala-N), centchroman (Chhaya), copper intrauterine devices including postpartum IUCD, emergency contraception and condoms, with eligibility, timing after childbirth and abortion, side effects and follow-up, using MoHFW reference manuals, FOGSI, WHO and MSF sources.

Centchroman twice weekly for 3 months then weekly, safe in breastfeeding, contraindications checked against FOGSI Pankh.
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg or ulipristal 30 mg up to 120 hours and copper IUD within 5 days checked against WHO (2021).

pathophysiology.summary: India's family planning programme offers a basket of free methods: condoms, combined pills (Mala-N), the weekly non-hormonal pill centchroman (Chhaya), the three-monthly injectable Antara (DMPA), copper IUCDs including immediate postpartum and post-abortion insertion, emergency contraceptive pills, and sterilisation. Good care starts with counselling about the woman's needs and medical eligibility, excludes pregnancy, and uses every contact — especially delivery and abortion — to offer a method. Most women can use most methods; key restrictions are oestrogen-containing pills in the first 6 weeks postpartum with breastfeeding, high blood pressure, migraine with aura, smoking over 35 and history of thrombosis. The right method is the one the woman will use: long-acting methods (IUCD, injectable) avoid daily adherence, while pills and condoms suit women who prefer control and quick return of fertility.
keyMechanisms: Combined pills suppress ovulation.
DMPA suppresses ovulation and thickens cervical mucus.
Centchroman is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator that prevents implantation.
Copper ions are toxic to sperm and prevent fertilisation; also work as emergency contraception.

clinicalManagement.title: Provide the method
actions: Offer PPIUCD or post-abortion IUCD at the time of delivery or abortion (MoHFW).
Breastfeeding: DMPA from 6 weeks postpartum (MoHFW). Not breastfeeding: DMPA from 4 weeks postpartum without backup (MoHFW; NHSRC).

clinicalManagement.title: Emergency contraception
actions: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg or ulipristal 30 mg as early as possible, up to 120 hours; copper IUD within 5 days is the most effective (WHO).

actions: DMPA bleeding: reassure; ibuprofen 400 mg or tranexamic acid 500 mg three times daily for 5 days, then ethinylestradiol 50 µg daily for 21 days if heavy; iron; refer if it persists (MoHFW).
Late DMPA return more than 4 months: pregnancy check, inject and use condoms for 7 days (MoHFW).
Migraine with aura on DMPA: stop MPA and switch to a non-oestrogen method; BP 160/100 mmHg or more or new thrombosis: stop oestrogen-containing methods and switch (MoHFW; MSF).

clinicalManagement.title: Follow-up
actions: IUCD at 6 weeks or after the first menstruation, whichever is earlier (MoHFW).
DMPA every 3 months; manage bleeding with NSAIDs or tranexamic acid (MoHFW).

vignette.text: Rekha, a 22-year-old woman from a village near Jaipur, delivered her first baby by normal vaginal birth 6 hours ago at a community health centre and is exclusively breastfeeding. She wants to wait at least 3 years before her next pregnancy but is worried that 'the copper-T causes cancer' and that injections will stop her milk. Her BP is 118/74 mmHg and she has no medical problems.

guidedApproach.title: How each method works, and why that matters
guidedApproach.prompt: Why does the mechanism change your advice?
guidedApproach.guidance: Combined pills such as Mala-N suppress ovulation through oestrogen and progestogen, so they work only when taken every day and carry oestrogen-related risks — thrombosis, raised blood pressure and stroke in women with migraine with aura or who smoke over 35. DMPA (Antara) suppresses ovulation for 3 months from a single injection, so adherence is easy, but return of fertility can take 7–10 months. Centchroman (Chhaya) is a non-steroidal selective oestrogen receptor modulator taken weekly after the first 3 months; it is safe during breastfeeding. Copper IUCDs are toxic to sperm and work for 5–10 years, and inserted within 5 days of unprotected sex they are the most effective emergency contraception.

guidedApproach.title: Eligibility and the warning signs
guidedApproach.prompt: What do you check before and after starting a method?
guidedApproach.guidance: Most women can use most methods, and no pelvic examination or blood test is needed before starting DMPA or pills. The key checks are pregnancy, blood pressure, migraine with aura, past thrombosis, smoking and breastfeeding status. Blood pressure of 160/100 mmHg or more, breastfeeding under 6 weeks and unexplained vaginal bleeding are category 4 conditions for DMPA. After insertion of an IUCD, teach the PAINS warning signs — period problems or pregnancy, abdominal pain, infection or discharge, not feeling well, and string problems. On DMPA, irregular bleeding and amenorrhoea are expected and are the commonest reason women stop, so counselling in advance improves continuation.

guidedApproach.title: When tests are needed
guidedApproach.prompt: Which investigations matter in contraceptive care?
guidedApproach.guidance: A urine pregnancy test is needed when pregnancy cannot be reasonably excluded, and after a late return for DMPA (more than 4 months since the last injection). Blood pressure is measured before starting oestrogen-containing pills and at follow-up. A speculum and bimanual examination is required before IUCD insertion to look for cervicitis or pelvic infection, and the strings are checked at the 6-week visit or after the first period. Missing strings need a pelvic ultrasound to distinguish expulsion from displacement or perforation. Routine bone density testing is not recommended for DMPA users.

guidedApproach.title: Using every contact to offer a method
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you make contraception happen in practice?
guidedApproach.guidance: The most effective moments are immediately after delivery and after abortion, when women are in contact with the health system. A post-placental or 48-hour PPIUCD, or a post-abortion IUCD within 12 days of a surgical abortion (around day 15 after a medical abortion, once completion is confirmed), gives years of protection without a separate visit. Breastfeeding women can start DMPA from 6 weeks and centchroman at any time; combined pills are avoided before 6 weeks and not recommended until 6 months. Emergency contraception should be offered whenever a woman reports unprotected sex in the past 5 days. Side effects are managed rather than used as a reason to stop: NSAIDs or tranexamic acid with iron for DMPA bleeding, and a switch of method when a contraindication appears. Every woman should hear that these methods do not protect against STIs or HIV.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 22-year-old woman delivered her first baby vaginally 6 hours ago and is exclusively breastfeeding. She wants to delay the next pregnancy for at least 3 years and has no medical problems. BP is 118/74 mmHg. She is willing to consider an IUCD after counselling.
boardQuestions.question: What is the best option to offer now?

options.explanation: Combined pills are contraindicated before 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women (MSF).
In breastfeeding women DMPA is started from 6 weeks postpartum (MoHFW).

options.text: Post-partum IUCD within 48 hours of delivery
options.explanation: Correct. PPIUCD can be inserted within 48 hours of vaginal delivery and gives long-acting protection (MoHFW IUCD manual).

options.text: No method until her periods return
options.explanation: Waiting misses the delivery opportunity; ovulation can return before the first period.
She has not had unprotected sex since delivery; she needs a regular method.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Use the immediate postpartum window for long-acting contraception.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: PPIUCD within 10 minutes of the placenta or within 48 hours of vaginal birth.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 30-year-old woman on DMPA returns for her injection 18 weeks after the last dose, having been away visiting family. She had unprotected sex once, 3 days ago, and no other sex in the previous 2 weeks. Her urine pregnancy test today is negative and she wants to continue DMPA.
boardQuestions.question: What should be done?

options.text: Give the injection and no further action
options.explanation: She is more than 4 months late (a 'dropout'); she needs backup and emergency contraception consideration.

options.text: Refuse the injection until her next period
options.explanation: This leaves her unprotected; she can be injected after pregnancy is reasonably excluded.

options.text: Switch to a combined pill only
options.explanation: Switching does not address the recent unprotected sex.

options.text: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg now, give the injection and advise condoms for 7 days
options.explanation: Correct. Late beyond 4 months: pregnancy check, inject, backup for 7 days (MoHFW). Levonorgestrel suits sex 3 days ago and, unlike ulipristal, does not require a 5-day wait before DMPA (WHO).
An IUCD within 5 days is effective emergency contraception, but the choice must follow counselling and consent.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Manage a late DMPA return safely.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: More than 4 months late: pregnancy check, inject, condoms 7 days; levonorgestrel if recent unprotected sex.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 36-year-old woman who smokes 15 bidis a day and has migraine preceded by flashing zigzag lights asks for 'the daily pill' because her sister uses it. She has two children aged 6 and 9, wants no more for now but is not ready for sterilisation, and has regular periods. BP is 132/84 mmHg and pelvic examination is normal.
boardQuestions.question: Which method is most appropriate to recommend?

options.explanation: Combined pills are contraindicated with migraine with neurological signs and in smokers over 35 (MSF).
Correct. A non-hormonal long-acting method avoids oestrogen risks and suits a woman wanting no more children for now (MoHFW).

options.text: Mala-N with aspirin to reduce stroke risk
options.explanation: Adding aspirin does not make combined pills safe in migraine with aura.
Repeated emergency pills are not a regular method.

options.text: No contraception until she stops smoking
options.explanation: She needs effective contraception now; several safe methods exist.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Identify contraindications to oestrogen and choose a safe alternative.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Migraine with aura or smoking over 35: avoid combined pills; offer IUCD, DMPA or other methods.

Return dates and warning signs for each method.

title: Delirium in adults (India)
specialty: Internal Medicine / Geriatrics / Psychiatry / Critical Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Prevention, recognition and treatment of delirium in adults in Indian hospitals and long-term care: risk factors, the 4AT and CAM-intensive care unit (ICU), multicomponent prevention, finding and treating causes, de-escalation and short-term drug treatment, using NICE CG103 (2010, updated 2023) and SIGN 157, because no Indian national delirium guideline could be opened.
findings: Risk factors (age 65 or over, cognitive impairment or dementia, hip fracture, severe illness), daily observation, 4AT (CAM-ICU or ICDSC in critical care), multicomponent prevention within 24 hours, treat causes, de-escalation first, short-term haloperidol usually 1 week or less at the lowest dose, caution in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia checked against NICE CG103.

Haloperidol 0.5–1 mg oral or 0.5 mg IM (maximum 2 mg in 24 hours), risperidone 0.25 mg (maximum 1 mg), lorazepam 0.5–1 mg (maximum 2 mg) when antipsychotics are contraindicated, review every 24 hours checked against SIGN 157.
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: Alcohol withdrawal delirium is covered in the Alcohol withdrawal (India) topic.
Baseline ECG before haloperidol is from an NHS prescribing tip citing MHRA, not from NICE or SIGN.
Midazolam IM is listed by SIGN but not included, to limit sedation risk on general wards.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness caused by a medical illness, drug or withdrawal. It affects many older inpatients and most ventilated patients, is often missed (especially the quiet, hypoactive form), and increases death, length of stay and later dementia. Prevention works: a familiar team, orientation, hydration, mobility, sleep, sensory aids, pain control and medicine review. When delirium develops, the priority is to find and treat the cause — infection, dehydration, drugs, retention, constipation, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance. Drugs are only for severe distress or risk, after de-escalation fails, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. In India, common precipitants in older inpatients include urinary and chest infection, dehydration, hyponatraemia, constipation, urinary retention, and drugs such as anticholinergics, opioids and benzodiazepines bought over the counter.
keyMechanisms: Acute brain dysfunction from inflammation, hypoperfusion, neurotransmitter imbalance (low acetylcholine, excess dopamine).
Vulnerable brains (dementia, old age) decompensate with small insults.
Anticholinergic and sedative drugs commonly precipitate delirium.
Antipsychotics reduce agitation but not duration and carry stroke and arrhythmia risk.

vignette.text: Mr K, an 82-year-old retired schoolteacher from Kolkata with mild memory problems, was admitted 2 days ago with a hip fracture after a fall. Last night he pulled out his cannula, shouted that the nurses were poisoning him and tried to climb out of bed. This morning he is drowsy and cannot say the months backwards. He has not opened his bowels for 4 days, has a palpable bladder, and is receiving tramadol and nightly diphenhydramine for sleep.

guidedApproach.title: Why the vulnerable brain fails
guidedApproach.prompt: Why do some patients become delirious with a minor insult?
guidedApproach.guidance: Delirium is acute brain failure. It results from an interaction between vulnerability — older age, dementia, frailty, sensory impairment, severe illness — and precipitating insults such as infection, surgery, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, pain, urinary retention, constipation and drugs. The more vulnerable the brain, the smaller the insult needed: a patient with dementia may become delirious from constipation alone. Inflammation, reduced cerebral perfusion and an imbalance between cholinergic and dopaminergic activity are thought to underlie it, which is why anticholinergic drugs (including many sleeping tablets and antihistamines) are such common culprits. Delirium increases the risk of death, longer hospital stay and later dementia, so prevention and early detection matter.

guidedApproach.title: Recognising the quiet and the noisy forms
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you spot delirium on a busy ward?
guidedApproach.guidance: The core features are an acute onset, a fluctuating course and inattention, with disorganised thinking or an altered level of consciousness. Hyperactive delirium — agitation, hallucinations, pulling out lines — is easy to see. Hypoactive delirium, with drowsiness, withdrawal and reduced intake, is common in older people and is often missed or mislabelled as depression or tiredness. Ask the family whether this is a change from normal: an informant history is the single most useful piece of information. Observe everyone at risk at least daily for changes in cognition, perception, physical function and behaviour, and use the 4AT when a change is noticed.

guidedApproach.title: Finding the cause
guidedApproach.prompt: What should the work-up include?
guidedApproach.guidance: Delirium is a symptom of something else, so the work-up is a search for the cause. Start at the bedside: check pain, look for a full bladder and constipation, measure oxygen saturation and glucose, and review the drug chart for new, increased or stopped medicines, especially anticholinergics, opioids, benzodiazepines and steroids. Blood tests should include sodium, calcium, urea, creatinine, liver function and a blood count, with cultures and a chest X-ray if infection is suspected. CT of the head is for focal signs, a fall, anticoagulation or no other explanation. An EEG helps when non-convulsive status epilepticus is possible. An ECG is needed before haloperidol to check the QTc interval.

guidedApproach.title: Treat the cause, protect the patient
guidedApproach.prompt: When and how should drugs be used?
guidedApproach.guidance: The treatment of delirium is the treatment of its cause, combined with good supportive care: a familiar team, reorientation with clocks and family, glasses and hearing aids, hydration and nutrition, mobilisation, bowel and bladder care, pain control and sleep. Drugs do not treat delirium. They are used only for severe distress or risk to the patient or others when verbal and non-verbal de-escalation has failed. Haloperidol 0.5–1 mg orally or 0.5 mg IM (maximum 2 mg in 24 hours; younger patients may need more, SIGN) is the usual choice, for a week or less, reviewed every 24 hours, with an ECG. In Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia, antipsychotics can cause severe rigidity, so lorazepam 0.5–1 mg is used instead. Stop or reduce deliriogenic drugs, and remember that sedation can mask deterioration.

boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Start haloperidol 2 mg three times daily
options.explanation: Drugs are not first-line; the dose also exceeds the 2 mg daily maximum (SIGN).

options.text: Treat the causes: catheterise the bladder, relieve constipation, stop diphenhydramine and review analgesia
options.explanation: Correct. Urinary retention, constipation, an anticholinergic and opioid exposure are likely precipitants (NICE 1.4, 1.7).
This is delirium, an acute change; cholinesterase inhibitors do not treat it.

options.text: Diazepam at night to improve sleep
options.explanation: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium except in withdrawal or when antipsychotics are contraindicated.
Delirium is a medical emergency managed on a medical or orthopaedic ward.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: Find and treat the cause: retention, constipation, drugs, pain, infection, hypoxia.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 76-year-old woman with Parkinson disease for 8 years is admitted with pneumonia and on the second night becomes very agitated and frightened, trying to hit staff and climb over the bed rails despite calm reassurance and her daughter staying with her. Her QTc is normal, oxygen saturation is 95% and she is on levodopa three times daily.
boardQuestions.question: Which drug is most appropriate if one is needed?

options.explanation: SIGN says do not use antipsychotics in Parkinson disease (NICE advises caution) because of severe extrapyramidal reactions.
Risperidone is also an antipsychotic and should be avoided with parkinsonism (SIGN).

options.text: Lorazepam 0.5–1 mg orally, maximum 2 mg in 24 hours
options.explanation: Correct. When antipsychotics are contraindicated, SIGN lists lorazepam at the lowest effective dose.
Stopping levodopa abruptly worsens rigidity and can cause a dangerous withdrawal syndrome.
Restraint increases harm and distress; de-escalation and safe drug choice come first.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Choose a safe drug when antipsychotics are contraindicated.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia: avoid antipsychotics; lorazepam if a drug is essential.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 70-year-old man on day 3 after abdominal surgery is quiet, eats little and sleeps most of the day. The nurses think he is 'just tired'. His daughter says he is not recognising her properly and was alert before surgery. His 4AT score is 6.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Depression does not cause fluctuating attention or a positive 4AT.
Fatigue does not impair recognition or produce a 4AT score of 6.
Dementia develops over months; this is an acute change after surgery.
Psychosis occurs with clear consciousness and intact attention.
Correct. Drowsiness, reduced intake and inattention with an acute change and a 4AT of 4 or more indicate hypoactive delirium (NICE 1.3, 1.6).

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Recognise hypoactive delirium.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Quiet, drowsy and new inattention = hypoactive delirium; use the 4AT.

evidenceAudit.scope: Lipid testing, cardiovascular risk categories, LDL-cholesterol and non-HDL targets, statins, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, inclisiran and management of hypertriglyceridaemia in Indian adults, built on the Cardiological Society of India (CSI) clinical practice guidelines for dyslipidaemia (2024).
findings: Risk categories (low, moderate, high, very high, extremely high), LDL-C targets (below 100, 100, 70 and 55 mg/dL) and non-HDL targets (below 130, 130, 100, 85 mg/dL), triglyceride below 150 and Lp(a) below 50 mg/dL, statin intensity doses (atorvastatin 40–80 mg high, 10–20 mg moderate; rosuvastatin 20–40 mg high, 5–10 mg moderate), ezetimibe 10 mg with statin early after acute coronary syndrome (ACS), non-statin therapy if LDL-C not below 55 mg/dL at 4 weeks, evolocumab 140 mg every 2 weeks or 420 mg monthly, inclisiran 284 mg at day 1, day 90 then 6-monthly, fenofibrate 145 mg for triglycerides above 500 mg/dL, icosapent ethyl 2 g twice daily, non-fasting lipid testing, lipid profile by age 18 and Lp(a) once checked against the CSI dyslipidaemia guideline executive summary (Indian Heart J 2024).

Bempedoic acid 180 mg once daily with maximally tolerated statin, no adjustment at eGFR 30 or above or in Child-Pugh A or B, and hyperuricaemia and tendon warnings checked against the Drugs.com dosage monograph (US label).
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: CSI gives no routine adult interval for repeat lipid testing and no CK threshold (section 5.1 advises against routine muscle and liver enzyme monitoring); the 4–12 week recheck and yearly review shown are general practice.
The extremely high-risk group has no numeric target in Table 1 of the executive summary; it is treated as at least the very high-risk target here.
The CSI summary notes South Asians may respond to lower statin doses (section 5.1); the US label suggests starting rosuvastatin at 5 mg in Asian patients.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Indians develop coronary artery disease about a decade earlier than many other populations, with atherogenic dyslipidaemia (high triglycerides, low HDL, small dense LDL) and high Lp(a). The CSI guideline asks for a lipid profile in everyone by 18 years (non-fasting is acceptable), Lp(a) once in a lifetime, risk categorisation by risk factors and established disease, and LDL-C targets that fall as risk rises — down to below 55 mg/dL in very high-risk patients. High-intensity statins are the foundation; ezetimibe, then PCSK9 inhibitors or inclisiran, are added when targets are not met. Very high triglycerides (above 500 mg/dL) are treated to prevent pancreatitis. Because risk is cumulative, the earlier and lower LDL-C is brought down, the larger the benefit; the CSI therefore asks for a first lipid profile by age 18 and cascade testing in families with premature disease.
keyMechanisms: LDL particles enter the artery wall and drive atherosclerosis; lowering LDL reduces events in proportion.
Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase; ezetimibe blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption; PCSK9 inhibitors increase LDL receptor recycling.
Lp(a) is inherited and independently causes coronary disease.
Very high triglycerides cause acute pancreatitis.

vignette.text: Mr P, a 44-year-old software engineer from Bengaluru, comes for a health check. His father had a heart attack at 48. He does not smoke, BP is 128/82 mmHg and HbA1c 5.6%. Total cholesterol is 312 mg/dL, LDL-C 228 mg/dL, HDL-C 42 mg/dL and triglycerides 140 mg/dL. You notice thickened Achilles tendons. He asks whether diet alone will fix it.

guidedApproach.title: Why LDL-C is the main target
guidedApproach.prompt: Why do guidelines focus on LDL-C and set lower targets for higher risk?
guidedApproach.guidance: Atherosclerosis begins when apolipoprotein B-containing particles, mainly LDL, enter the arterial wall and are retained and oxidised, attracting macrophages that form foam cells and plaques. The amount of plaque reflects both the LDL-C level and how long the artery has been exposed, so a person with familial hypercholesterolaemia carries a decade's extra exposure by middle age. Trials of statins, ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitors all show that lowering LDL-C reduces events in proportion to the fall, without a clear lower threshold — hence the targets fall from below 100 to below 55 mg/dL as risk rises. Indians often have atherogenic dyslipidaemia with high triglycerides and low HDL-C, and about one in four South Asians has a raised Lp(a), which is inherited and not lowered by lifestyle.

guidedApproach.title: Spotting the high-risk patient
guidedApproach.prompt: Who needs more than a routine check?
guidedApproach.guidance: Most people with dyslipidaemia have no symptoms, so the diagnosis is made by testing and by recognising risk. Ask about premature coronary disease in first-degree relatives (men under 55, women under 60), smoking or tobacco chewing, hypertension and diabetes and its duration. Examine for tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma and corneal arcus at a young age, which suggest familial hypercholesterolaemia, and for eruptive xanthomas with very high triglycerides. Look for secondary causes — hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, poorly controlled diabetes and drugs such as steroids — because treating them can correct the lipids.

guidedApproach.title: What to measure and when
guidedApproach.prompt: Which tests does the CSI recommend?
guidedApproach.guidance: A standard lipid profile (total cholesterol, LDL-C, HDL-C, non-HDL-C and triglycerides) can be taken non-fasting for risk estimation and treatment decisions. Everyone should have a profile by age 18, and Lp(a) should be measured at least once in a lifetime; a value above 50 mg/dL marks extra inherited risk. Check TSH, glucose or HbA1c, creatinine, liver tests and urine protein to exclude secondary causes before starting lifelong treatment. After starting or changing therapy, repeat the lipids at 4–12 weeks to confirm the target is met, then yearly. Check CK and TSH if muscle symptoms appear. Cascade testing of relatives is advised in familial hypercholesterolaemia and premature coronary disease.

guidedApproach.title: Statins first, then add-ons
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you reach the target?
guidedApproach.guidance: Lifestyle change matters for everyone but rarely reaches targets alone in high-risk patients. The CSI places people in risk categories and sets LDL-C targets of below 100, 70 or 55 mg/dL. High and very high-risk patients start a high-intensity statin — atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg — and South Asians may respond well to lower doses. After an acute coronary syndrome, ezetimibe is added from the start. If the target is not met at 4–12 weeks, add ezetimibe 10 mg, then a PCSK9 inhibitor or inclisiran in very high-risk patients. Triglycerides above 500 mg/dL need fenofibrate to prevent pancreatitis; for persistently raised triglycerides in ASCVD or diabetes, icosapent ethyl reduces events. Statin side effects are usually manageable with a dose or drug change rather than stopping.

pathophysiology.summary: Urticaria (hives) is itchy wheals that come and go within 24 hours; angioedema is deeper swelling of lips, eyelids, tongue or genitals lasting up to 3 days. Acute urticaria is usually triggered by infection, drugs (NSAIDs, paracetamol, ACE inhibitors) or food. Chronic urticaria lasting over 6 weeks is usually spontaneous, sometimes inducible by pressure, cold, heat or sun, and rarely needs tests. Treatment is a daily non-sedating antihistamine, increased up to four times the standard dose, then add-on therapy in tertiary care. Throat swelling, breathing difficulty or shock means anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline first. Angioedema without wheals raises the possibility of hereditary angioedema or ACE-inhibitor angioedema. In India, chronic spontaneous urticaria is common in young women, and long courses of oral steroids and sedating antihistamines bought over the counter are frequent and harmful.
keyMechanisms: Mast cell degranulation releases histamine, causing wheals and itch.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria is often autoimmune (antibodies against IgE or its receptor).
Hereditary and ACE-inhibitor angioedema are bradykinin-mediated and do not respond to antihistamines.
Second-generation antihistamines block H1 receptors with little sedation.

vignette.text: Ms F, a 29-year-old bank clerk from Hyderabad, has had itchy red wheals on her trunk and arms almost daily for 4 months. Each wheal fades within a few hours without a mark, and twice her lips have swollen overnight. She has taken prednisolone courses from a local clinic 'whenever it is bad' and chlorphenamine at night, which makes her drowsy at work. She has no breathing difficulty and takes no regular medicines.

guidedApproach.title: Mast cells, histamine and why antihistamines are updosed
guidedApproach.prompt: Why does chronic urticaria respond to higher antihistamine doses?
guidedApproach.guidance: Wheals and angioedema are caused by mast cell degranulation in the skin, releasing histamine and other mediators that make vessels leak. In chronic spontaneous urticaria the trigger is often autoimmune — antibodies against IgE or its receptor activate mast cells repeatedly — rather than an allergy to a food or drug, so extensive allergy testing rarely helps. Second-generation antihistamines block H1 receptors without much sedation, and because the mast cell drive is persistent, higher doses (up to four times the standard) control symptoms in many patients who do not respond to standard doses. Bradykinin-mediated angioedema — hereditary or due to ACE inhibitors — involves a different pathway, which is why antihistamines and steroids do not work for it.

guidedApproach.title: Recognise the emergency and the mimics
guidedApproach.prompt: Which features change management?
guidedApproach.guidance: First decide whether this is anaphylaxis: wheals with breathing difficulty, throat tightness, hypotension, collapse or gastrointestinal symptoms need IM adrenaline at once. Then decide the type: acute urticaria (under 6 weeks) is often triggered by infection, drugs or food; chronic urticaria lasts more than 6 weeks and is usually spontaneous, sometimes inducible by pressure, cold, heat, sun or exercise. Individual wheals should last under 24 hours and leave normal skin. Lesions that last longer, burn, or leave bruising suggest urticarial vasculitis and need a biopsy. Angioedema without wheals points to an ACE inhibitor or hereditary angioedema.

guidedApproach.title: Why fewer tests are better
guidedApproach.prompt: What should you test for?
guidedApproach.guidance: In most patients the diagnosis is clinical and no tests are needed. Investigations are guided by history and examination: a skin biopsy when lesions persist beyond 24–48 hours or bruise, C4 and C1-inhibitor levels when angioedema occurs without wheals, and infection testing only when the history suggests it. Blood tests are needed before immunosuppressive treatment such as ciclosporin. Thyroid tests, autologous serum skin tests and skin-prick or IgE tests have limited value. Explaining this to patients avoids expensive and unhelpful testing and redirects attention to effective treatment.

guidedApproach.title: The antihistamine ladder
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you treat chronic urticaria step by step?
guidedApproach.guidance: Start a once-daily non-sedating antihistamine — cetirizine 10 mg, levocetirizine 5 mg, loratadine 10 mg or fexofenadine 180 mg — and take it every day, not only when itching. If symptoms persist after 2 weeks, increase the dose up to fourfold. If still uncontrolled after a further 2–4 weeks, specialist care adds omalizumab 300 mg every 4 weeks, ciclosporin 3–5 mg/kg or montelukast 10 mg. Avoid long-term sedating antihistamines and repeated oral steroids; a short prednisolone course (0.3–0.5 mg/kg for up to 10 days) is only for severe flares. Children receive weight- and age-appropriate cetirizine doses. Anaphylaxis is treated with IM adrenaline 0.2–0.5 mg in adults or 0.01 mg/kg (maximum 0.3 mg) in children, repeated every 5–15 minutes as needed.

options.explanation: Correct. This is first- and second-line treatment for chronic urticaria (ICMR STW).
Omalizumab is third-line in tertiary care after antihistamine updosing fails.

options.text: Increase chlorphenamine to three times daily
options.explanation: Long-term first-generation antihistamines are avoided because of sedation (ICMR STW).

boardQuestions.vignette: A 58-year-old man on ramipril for 3 years presents with marked swelling of the lips and tongue for 6 hours. He has no wheals or itch. He is breathing comfortably with SpO2 98% and BP 142/88 mmHg. Antihistamine and hydrocortisone given 2 hours ago made no difference.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most likely cause and key action?

options.text: Chronic spontaneous urticaria; increase antihistamine fourfold
options.explanation: There are no wheals, and antihistamines have failed; this pattern suggests bradykinin-mediated angioedema.

options.text: ACE-inhibitor angioedema; stop ramipril permanently and monitor the airway
options.explanation: Correct. Angioedema without wheals in a patient on an ACE inhibitor, unresponsive to antihistamines, is typical; ACE inhibitors are drugs to avoid (ICMR STW).
Contact dermatitis is eczematous and does not cause tongue swelling.
Allergic angioedema usually comes with wheals or itch and responds to antihistamines.
Bites do not cause this pattern of lip and tongue swelling.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: Angioedema without wheals: think ACE inhibitor or hereditary angioedema; antihistamines often fail.

evidenceAudit.scope: Chickenpox and shingles in adults and children in India: diagnosis, complications and red flags, oral and IV acyclovir, valacyclovir, pain and post-herpetic neuralgia, pregnancy, eye involvement, isolation and referral, built on the ICMR Varicella and Herpes Zoster STW (July 2022).

Not clinically reviewed.

NACI 2016: VarIg 125 IU per 10 kg, maximum 625 IU, ideally within 96 hours and up to 10 days. CDC 2013: IM; minimum 62.5 IU at 2 kg or less and 125 IU at 2.1–10 kg; observe for 28 days; contraindicated after severe reaction to immune globulin or IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies.

UKHSA 2023: oral aciclovir 800 mg four times daily (children 10 mg/kg, maximum 800 mg) or valaciclovir 1 g three times daily (children 20 mg/kg, maximum 1 g) from day 7 to day 14 after exposure is first choice for susceptible pregnant and immunosuppressed contacts; VZIG for neonates exposed within a week of delivery or when antivirals are unsuitable.
unverifiedSections: Isolation duration is not specified in the STW (usually until all lesions crust).

Post-exposure antiviral prophylaxis is from UKHSA (2023) and VarIg details from CDC (2013) and NACI (2016), because the ICMR STW only says VarIg may be considered when vaccination is contraindicated; VarIg may be hard to obtain in India. Renal doses are from the US labels (Drugs.com).
Famciclovir is not mentioned in the STW.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Chickenpox (varicella) is a highly contagious childhood infection that is more severe in adults, pregnant women, newborns and the immunocompromised. Shingles (herpes zoster) is reactivation of the same virus in a dermatome, commonest in older and immunosuppressed people, and its main long-term problem is post-herpetic neuralgia. Diagnosis is clinical. Oral acyclovir started early (within 24 hours of rash for varicella, 72 hours for zoster) shortens illness; IV acyclovir is for complicated disease. Eye involvement (lesions on the forehead or nose tip) needs urgent ophthalmology. Avoid aspirin in children. Susceptible high-risk contacts — pregnant women, newborns and the immunocompromised — need post-exposure immune globulin, and patients remain infectious until all lesions have crusted. Varicella pneumonia, encephalitis and secondary bacterial infection are the main causes of death.
keyMechanisms: Primary infection spreads by droplets and vesicle fluid; incubation 10–21 days.
Virus becomes latent in sensory ganglia; waning immunity allows reactivation as zoster.
Acyclovir inhibits viral DNA polymerase after activation by viral thymidine kinase.
Nerve damage causes post-herpetic neuralgia.

symptoms: Prodrome of fever and headache 1–2 days before the rash (adults)
Eye pain, red eye or blurred vision (zoster ophthalmicus)
physicalSigns: Vesicles on red base in crops at different stages (dew drop on a rose petal) (ICMR STW)
Grouped vesicles in one dermatome (ICMR STW)
Lesions on forehead or nose tip (ophthalmicus) (ICMR STW)
Facial palsy with vesicles in the ear canal (Ramsay Hunt syndrome)
redFlags: Breathlessness or chest pain (pneumonia) (ICMR STW)
Neck stiffness or confusion (encephalitis) (ICMR STW)
Haemorrhagic or necrotic lesions; multi-dermatomal or disseminated zoster (ICMR STW)
Haemodynamic instability (ICMR STW)
Pregnancy, newborn or immunosuppression
precipitants: Pregnancy, newborn of a mother with peripartum varicella, no prior chickenpox or vaccination

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Small oval vesicles on palms, soles and mouth in young children, not in crops on the trunk; clinical diagnosis.
Honey-coloured crusts around nose and mouth without crops of vesicles; Gram stain or culture settles it.
Grouped vesicles that recur at the same site, not following a dermatome; viral PCR of a vesicle settles it.
Itchy papules with a central punctum on exposed skin, no fever or crops; history settles it.
Recurrent, multidermatomal or severe zoster in a young adult; HIV testing settles it (general practice).
Deep lesions all at the same stage, often on palms, soles or genitals, with tender lymph nodes; PCR of lesion fluid settles it.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Fever with generalised vesicles in different stages.

Systemic complications, haemorrhagic varicella, immunosuppression, neonatal varicella, disseminated zoster.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess
actions: Look for red flags, pregnancy, immunosuppression and eye involvement (ICMR STW).
Ask about high-risk contacts at home (pregnant, newborn, immunosuppressed) who may need VarIg (NACI).

clinicalManagement.title: Varicella
actions: Oral acyclovir within 24 hours of rash for infants, children over 12, adults, pregnant women and the immunosuppressed; IV acyclovir for complications (ICMR STW). Healthy children aged 1–12 get symptomatic care.
Paracetamol for fever; antihistamine; daily bath; avoid aspirin (ICMR STW).
Isolate from high-risk contacts (ICMR STW).
Pregnancy: treat with acyclovir and refer; infection in the first 20 weeks may cause congenital varicella syndrome, and perinatal maternal varicella may cause neonatal varicella (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Herpes zoster
actions: Acyclovir or valacyclovir for 7 days; later if new lesions, ophthalmicus or Ramsay Hunt (ICMR STW).
NSAIDs for pain; add pregabalin, gabapentin or a tricyclic if uncontrolled (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Protect exposed contacts
actions: Susceptible pregnant or immunosuppressed contacts: oral aciclovir 800 mg four times daily (or valaciclovir 1 g three times daily) from day 7 to day 14 after exposure (UKHSA).
Neonates exposed within a week of delivery, or when antivirals are unsuitable: VarIg 125 IU per 10 kg IM, maximum 625 IU, as soon as possible and within 10 days; observe for 28 days (NACI; CDC).
Prevention: live varicella vaccine at 12–15 months and 4–6 years, 2 doses for those 13 and over; zoster vaccine may be offered over 50 years (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer
actions: Eye involvement: ophthalmology; ear lesions or facial weakness (Ramsay Hunt): ENT (ICMR STW).
Complications, immunosuppression, haemorrhagic varicella, failure of oral acyclovir, neonatal varicella, multidermatomal or disseminated zoster, post-herpetic neuralgia (ICMR STW).

vignette.text: Mrs S, a 26-year-old schoolteacher from Pune who is 20 weeks pregnant, phones because her 5-year-old son developed an itchy blistering rash yesterday. She does not remember having chickenpox and has not been vaccinated. She feels well. Her son has fever and crops of vesicles on his trunk, with new crops still appearing. Her elderly father, who lives with them, is on chemotherapy for lymphoma.

guidedApproach.title: Primary infection, latency and reactivation
guidedApproach.prompt: Why does the same virus cause two diseases?
guidedApproach.guidance: Varicella zoster virus enters through the respiratory tract, replicates in lymphoid tissue and spreads in the blood to the skin, producing crops of vesicles at different stages. It is infectious from about 2 days before the rash until all lesions crust. The virus then becomes latent in sensory ganglia. When cell-mediated immunity falls — with age, HIV, cancer or steroids — it reactivates and travels down one sensory nerve, causing dermatomal pain followed by vesicles (zoster). Nerve inflammation explains post-herpetic neuralgia. Severe disease in adults, pregnancy and immunosuppression reflects the importance of T-cell immunity in controlling the virus.

guidedApproach.title: Spot the complications early
guidedApproach.prompt: Which features change management?
guidedApproach.guidance: In varicella, look for breathlessness or chest pain (pneumonia, especially in adults, smokers and pregnant women), confusion or ataxia (encephalitis, cerebellitis), haemorrhagic lesions and secondary bacterial infection. In zoster, lesions on the forehead, nose tip or eye suggest ophthalmic involvement (Hutchinson's sign) and need urgent ophthalmology; facial palsy with ear vesicles is Ramsay Hunt syndrome. Zoster in more than one dermatome, dissemination, or recurrent zoster in a young adult should prompt HIV testing. Ask every patient about pregnant, newborn and immunosuppressed contacts.

guidedApproach.title: Clinical diagnosis, tests for doubt
guidedApproach.prompt: When do you test?
guidedApproach.guidance: Most varicella and zoster are diagnosed clinically. Testing is useful when the rash is atypical, in immunosuppressed patients, or in pregnancy: vesicle fluid PCR is the most sensitive test. Varicella IgG serology confirms immunity in an exposed pregnant woman or immunocompromised contact with uncertain history, but should not delay VarIg beyond the window. A chest X-ray assesses suspected pneumonia, and lumbar puncture suspected encephalitis. HIV testing is advised in recurrent or severe zoster. Renal function guides acyclovir dosing in older adults and those receiving IV treatment.

guidedApproach.title: Antivirals, analgesia and protecting contacts
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you treat and protect?
guidedApproach.guidance: Start oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 5–7 days in adults, adolescents, pregnant women and the immunosuppressed within 24 hours of varicella rash (children under 40 kg 20 mg/kg four times daily, maximum 800 mg). For zoster, acyclovir 800 mg five times daily or valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days, ideally within 72 hours, or later if new lesions or eye involvement. Complicated or immunosuppressed patients need IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours with hydration. Treat pain with an NSAID and add pregabalin, gabapentin or amitriptyline for neuropathic pain. Avoid aspirin in children. Susceptible pregnant or immunosuppressed contacts receive oral aciclovir or valaciclovir from day 7 to 14 after exposure, and exposed newborns VarIg 125 IU per 10 kg IM.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 26-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant was exposed yesterday to her son's chickenpox at home. She has no history of chickenpox or vaccination, is well, and her varicella IgG is negative. Her kidney function is normal and she has no other illness. She asks whether she needs any treatment.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate management?

options.explanation: Live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy, so this is unsafe.

options.text: Reassure; treat only if a rash develops
options.explanation: A susceptible pregnant woman is high risk and should be offered prophylaxis (UKHSA).

options.text: Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily starting today for 7 days
options.explanation: Prophylactic antivirals are given from day 7 to day 14 after exposure, not straight away (UKHSA).

options.text: Oral aciclovir 800 mg four times daily from day 7 to day 14 after exposure
options.explanation: Correct. Antivirals are now first choice for susceptible pregnant contacts; VarIg is for those who cannot take them (UKHSA).
Exposure alone is not an indication; congenital varicella risk is low.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Protect a susceptible pregnant contact.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Susceptible pregnant contact: oral antiviral from day 7 to 14; VarIg if antivirals unsuitable.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 68-year-old man has had burning pain over his right forehead for 3 days and now has vesicles on the forehead and the tip of his nose. His right eye is red and watering. He has diabetes and creatinine is normal.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily and urgent ophthalmology review
options.explanation: Correct. Nose-tip lesions suggest ophthalmic involvement, so antiviral treatment and urgent eye review are needed (ICMR STW).
Topical treatment does not prevent eye complications from zoster ophthalmicus.
Analgesia is needed but does not treat the virus or protect the eye.

options.text: Give an antiviral only if new lesions appear
options.explanation: Eye involvement needs antiviral treatment now, whether or not new lesions appear (ICMR STW).
Steroids alone without antivirals are not recommended in zoster.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Recognise and treat zoster ophthalmicus.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Nose-tip vesicles: think eye involvement and refer urgently.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 30-year-old man has had chickenpox for 3 days. Today he is breathless, with SpO2 89% on air, respiratory rate 30/min and bilateral crackles. Chest X-ray shows diffuse nodular shadows. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and weighs 70 kg.
boardQuestions.question: What is the best treatment?

options.text: Oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily at home
options.explanation: Pneumonia is a complication needing admission and IV treatment.

options.text: Oral valacyclovir 1 g three times daily
options.explanation: Oral treatment is inadequate for life-threatening varicella pneumonia.

options.text: Admit; IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg (700 mg) every 8 hours with oxygen
options.explanation: Correct. Varicella pneumonia needs IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours and supportive care (ICMR STW).
VarIg is prophylaxis for exposed contacts, not treatment of established disease.
Aspirin is avoided in varicella and fluids alone do not treat the infection.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Treat complicated varicella with IV acyclovir.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Varicella pneumonia: admit and give IV acyclovir.

pathophysiology.summary: Bradyarrhythmias range from harmless sinus bradycardia in athletes to complete heart block causing syncope, heart failure or death. In India, common causes are degenerative conduction disease in older people, drugs (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin), hyperkalaemia in kidney disease, hypothyroidism and inferior myocardial infarction. The ICMR workflow asks clinicians to identify symptomatic bradycardia below 50/min, look for instability, withhold offending drugs, treat hyperkalaemia, and arrange temporary pacing when needed, then permanent pacing for persistent high-grade block or symptomatic sinus node disease. Atropine is the first drug; isoprenaline or adrenaline infusions and transcutaneous pacing bridge to transvenous pacing. Bradycardia matters when it causes low output: the key bedside question is whether the patient is unstable, not the absolute rate, and the second is whether the escape rhythm is likely to fail.
keyMechanisms: Sinus node dysfunction: failure of impulse generation (pauses, slow rates).
AV block: failure of conduction from atria to ventricles; Mobitz II and complete block are infranodal and unstable.
Atropine blocks vagal tone and works for nodal but not infranodal block.
Beta-agonists (isoprenaline, adrenaline) increase rate and conduction.

vignette.text: Mr R, a 72-year-old retired farmer from Nagpur, is brought to the emergency department after fainting twice at home. He takes metoprolol 50 mg twice daily and amlodipine for hypertension, and has diabetic kidney disease. His pulse is 34/min and regular, BP 84/50 mmHg, and he is drowsy but rousable. The ECG shows complete heart block with a broad QRS escape rhythm.

guidedApproach.title: Where the conduction fails and why it matters
guidedApproach.prompt: How does the level of block predict risk?
guidedApproach.guidance: The sinus node sets the rate and the AV node and His–Purkinje system conduct it. Sinus node disease and AV nodal block (first degree, Mobitz I) often reflect vagal tone, drugs or ischaemia of the inferior wall, and the escape rhythm from the AV junction is narrow and reasonably fast, so the risk of asystole is lower. Block below the AV node (Mobitz II, complete block with a broad QRS) relies on a slow, unreliable ventricular escape, which can fail suddenly, so these patients need pacing even when they look stable. Hyperkalaemia, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers and digoxin depress both the node and conduction, and in older Indian patients with kidney disease these often combine.

guidedApproach.title: Unstable versus stable
guidedApproach.prompt: Which features decide the urgency?
guidedApproach.guidance: The rate alone does not decide treatment. Look for adverse features: shock or systolic BP below 90 mmHg, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, heart failure and impaired consciousness. Any of these makes the patient unstable and needs immediate treatment. Then look for asystole risk: recent asystole, Mobitz II, complete block with a broad QRS, or ventricular pauses over 3 seconds. A patient with neither may only need the cause treated and observation. Remember Cushing's response — bradycardia with hypertension and reduced consciousness points to raised intracranial pressure and needs a CT of the head, not atropine.

guidedApproach.title: The ECG and the reversible causes
guidedApproach.prompt: What do you check first?
guidedApproach.guidance: A 12-lead ECG identifies the rhythm and level of block and may show inferior ST elevation, peaked T waves of hyperkalaemia or digoxin effect. Send potassium, creatinine, glucose, troponin and thyroid function; a digoxin level when relevant. Review every medicine including eye drops (timolol). Echocardiography assesses structural disease. A Holter monitor captures intermittent block in a stable patient with symptoms. Treating hyperkalaemia or stopping a beta-blocker may make pacing unnecessary, which is why the causes are checked before a permanent pacemaker is planned.

guidedApproach.title: Drugs as a bridge to pacing
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you treat unstable bradycardia step by step?
guidedApproach.guidance: Give atropine 500 micrograms IV (RCUK; AHA uses 1 mg), repeating every 3–5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg. Atropine works on the AV node and often fails in infranodal block or after heart transplant. If there is no response, start an isoprenaline infusion at 5 micrograms/min, an adrenaline infusion at 2–10 micrograms/min or a dopamine infusion at 5–20 micrograms/kg/min, or begin transcutaneous pacing with analgesia and sedation. Treat hyperkalaemia with 10 mL 10% calcium gluconate. In beta-blocker toxicity, glucagon 5 mg IV can be added after fluids and vasopressors. All of these are a bridge to transvenous pacing and then a permanent pacemaker when block persists.

boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.explanation: He is unstable with shock and reduced consciousness, so waiting is unsafe.

options.text: Atropine 500 micrograms IV while preparing an infusion or pacing
options.explanation: Correct. Atropine is first, but broad-complex complete block often fails to respond, so prepare pacing (RCUK; ICMR STW).

options.explanation: Rate-slowing drugs should be withheld in symptomatic bradycardia (ICMR STW).

boardQuestions.vignette: A 24-year-old marathon runner has a pulse of 42/min at a pre-employment check. He has no symptoms, BP is 118/70 mmHg, and he has never fainted. The ECG shows sinus bradycardia with no block, and his rate rises to 110/min on climbing stairs.
boardQuestions.question: What is the best management?

options.explanation: Atropine is for symptomatic bradycardia with adverse features, which he does not have.
There are no pacing indications without symptoms or high-grade block (ICMR STW).
There is no instability or asystole risk, so pacing is not indicated.
Correct. Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia with a normal chronotropic response in an athlete is physiological.
Infusions are a bridge for unstable patients who fail atropine.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: Treat the patient, not the rate: asymptomatic athletes need no treatment.

Risperidone SmPC 4.1–4.4: 0.25 mg twice daily, increase by 0.25 mg twice daily no more often than every other day; optimum 0.5 mg twice daily, up to 1 mg twice daily; no longer than 6 weeks; halve doses in renal or hepatic impairment; increased mortality and about 3-fold cerebrovascular risk in elderly people with dementia; not for dementias other than Alzheimer.

pathophysiology.summary: Dementia affects millions of older Indians, most undiagnosed, and is often dismissed as normal ageing. It is a progressive decline in memory and at least one other cognitive domain severe enough to affect daily function. The ICMR workflow asks primary care doctors to suspect it from the history given by a close caregiver, to rule out delirium and depression, to look for treatable causes (thyroid, B12, syphilis, HIV, subdural haematoma, normal pressure hydrocephalus), and to start a cholinesterase inhibitor for Alzheimer or mixed dementia, adding memantine in moderate to severe disease. Behavioural symptoms are managed first without drugs. Caregiver education, support and planning for palliative care are core. Alzheimer disease is the commonest type, followed by vascular and mixed dementia; the diagnosis is clinical and supported, not made, by tests.
keyMechanisms: Alzheimer disease: amyloid plaques and tau tangles with loss of cholinergic neurons.
Vascular dementia: multiple infarcts or small vessel disease; common in India with hypertension and diabetes.
Cholinesterase inhibitors increase acetylcholine; memantine blocks excess glutamate (NMDA) activity.
Delirium on top of dementia accelerates decline.

vignette.text: Mr K, a 74-year-old retired railway clerk from Lucknow, is brought by his daughter, who says that over 2 years he has repeated questions, got lost returning from the market and stopped managing his pension. He now shouts at his wife in the evenings and once pushed her. He has hypertension and diabetes. There is no fever, no recent fall and no sudden change.

guidedApproach.title: Neurodegeneration and vascular injury
guidedApproach.prompt: What causes the decline, and why do the drugs help only a little?
guidedApproach.guidance: In Alzheimer disease, amyloid plaques and tau tangles cause loss of neurons and synapses, starting in the hippocampus and spreading to temporal and parietal cortex; this explains early memory loss and later language and visuospatial problems. Loss of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain reduces acetylcholine, which is why cholinesterase inhibitors give modest symptomatic benefit without changing the course. Glutamate excitotoxicity underlies the use of memantine. Vascular dementia results from strokes and small-vessel disease, often with stepwise decline and gait problems, and hypertension and diabetes are key modifiable risks in India. Mixed pathology is common in older people.

guidedApproach.title: History from the caregiver
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you recognise dementia and its subtype?
guidedApproach.guidance: Dementia is diagnosed when decline in memory and at least one other domain — language, attention, executive function or visuospatial skill — affects daily function. The history from a close caregiver is more reliable than the patient's own account. Ask how it began and progressed: gradual memory loss suggests Alzheimer disease, stepwise decline with focal signs suggests vascular dementia, early hallucinations and parkinsonism suggest Lewy body disease, and early personality change suggests frontotemporal dementia. Always look for delirium (acute, fluctuating) and depression, and for red flags such as fever, rapid progression, seizures or head injury that need urgent referral.

guidedApproach.title: Look for the reversible
guidedApproach.prompt: Which tests matter?
guidedApproach.guidance: Basic tests at primary care look for treatable contributors: blood count, glucose, renal and liver function, electrolytes, TSH, vitamin B12, VDRL and HIV. These rarely reverse dementia but often make it worse when present. A brief cognitive screening test documents a baseline for later comparison; the STW names no specific tool, so use one validated in the patient's language. Neuroimaging (CT or MRI) at district level excludes subdural haematoma, tumours and normal pressure hydrocephalus and shows vascular disease. A rapid course or young onset needs specialist assessment for rarer causes.

guidedApproach.title: Drugs, behaviour and the caregiver
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you manage dementia step by step?
guidedApproach.guidance: Start donepezil 5 mg once daily for a month, then 10 mg, in Alzheimer or mixed dementia; use rivastigmine or galantamine if it is not tolerated. Add memantine 5 mg twice daily, rising to 10 mg twice daily, in moderate to severe disease. Treat depression with escitalopram 10 mg. Manage behavioural symptoms first by finding triggers — pain, constipation, infection, poor sleep — and with non-drug measures. If aggression in Alzheimer dementia persists with risk of harm, risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily (usually 0.5 mg twice daily, maximum 1 mg twice daily) may be used for no more than 6 weeks, accepting the increased stroke and mortality risk; avoid it in Lewy body and vascular dementia. Support and educate the caregiver.

boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate treatment?

boardQuestions.vignette: A 76-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer dementia has hit his wife repeatedly over 3 weeks despite pain relief, treatment of constipation, a structured routine and caregiver training. He takes donepezil 10 mg daily and has no parkinsonism or hallucinations. Creatinine and liver tests are normal. His wife is frightened and asks for help.
boardQuestions.question: Which treatment is most appropriate?

options.text: Risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily, titrated slowly, for no more than 6 weeks
options.explanation: Correct. Risperidone is licensed short term for persistent aggression in Alzheimer dementia after non-drug measures fail (SmPC 4.1–4.2).

options.explanation: High-dose, long-term typical antipsychotics cause severe parkinsonism and falls.
Regular benzodiazepines worsen confusion, sedation and falls in dementia.
This exceeds the 1 mg twice daily maximum and the 6-week limit (SmPC 4.2).
Stopping the cholinesterase inhibitor does not treat aggression and may worsen cognition.
